selftest.q: HLD 1 · What happens, step by step, between typing https://example.com and seeing the page?
selftest.a: DNS turns the name into an IP address. The browser opens a TCP connection to that IP, and TLS sets up encryption on top. It sends an HTTP request. The server runs code, often reads a database, and sends back an HTTP response. The browser renders it.

selftest.q: HLD 2 · Why put a load balancer in front of several servers, and what must be true of the servers behind it?
selftest.a: To spread requests across servers and keep working when one dies. The servers should be stateless: no user session kept in one server's memory, so any server can answer any request. Session data lives in a shared store such as Redis or the database.

selftest.q: HLD 3 · What is the cache-aside pattern?
selftest.a: The app asks the cache first. On a miss it reads the database, puts the result in the cache with an expiry time (TTL), and returns it. On a write it updates the database and deletes the cached copy so the next read refills it.

selftest.q: HLD 4 · When would you pick a SQL database, and when a NoSQL one?
selftest.a: SQL when data has relations, you need transactions (all-or-nothing writes) and flexible queries, such as orders and payments. NoSQL (key-value or document) when access is mostly by one key at very large scale, or the shape of the data changes often.

selftest.q: HLD 5 · A user saves their profile, reloads, and sees the old version. The database has replicas. What probably happened, and one fix?
selftest.a: The read went to a replica that had not yet copied the write (replication lag). Fix: send that user's reads to the main (leader) database for a short time after they write, which is called read-your-writes.

selftest.q: LLD 1 · What does the Single Responsibility Principle say?
selftest.a: A class should have one reason to change: one job. A class that formats invoices and also emails them has two reasons to change, so split it.

selftest.q: LLD 2 · Inheritance or composition: what is the difference, and which do you reach for first?
selftest.a: Inheritance says a class is a kind of its parent and reuses the parent's code. Composition says a class has other objects and calls them. Prefer composition: parts can be swapped at runtime and you avoid deep, brittle class trees.

selftest.q: LLD 3 · What is the Strategy pattern? Give one example.
selftest.a: Several interchangeable ways of doing one job, each behind the same interface, picked at runtime. Example: a checkout that takes a pricing strategy (regular, festive sale, member discount) without an if-else chain.

selftest.q: LLD 4 · Why do many reviewers push back on the Singleton pattern?
selftest.a: It is global state in disguise. Code that uses it hides that dependency, tests can't swap it for a fake easily, and it can cause trouble with threads. Passing the object in is usually better.

selftest.q: LLD 5 · Design a parking lot: name the main classes and what each one does.
selftest.a: ParkingLot (holds levels, entry point), Level (holds spots), Spot (size, free or taken), Vehicle with types (bike, car, truck), Ticket (vehicle, spot, entry time), a spot-finding strategy, and a fee calculator. A good answer keeps fee rules and spot choice swappable.

selftest.q: AI 1 · What is the difference between supervised and unsupervised learning?
selftest.a: Supervised learning trains on examples that come with the right answer (a label), such as emails marked spam or not. Unsupervised learning has no labels and finds structure, such as grouping similar customers.

selftest.q: AI 2 · What is overfitting, and two ways to reduce it?
selftest.a: The model memorises the training data, noise included, so it does well on training data and badly on new data. Reduce it with more data, a simpler model, regularisation, or early stopping when the validation score stops improving.

selftest.q: AI 3 · Precision and recall: what does each one measure?
selftest.a: Precision: of everything the model flagged, how much was really positive. Recall: of all the real positives, how many the model caught. A spam filter that flags very little tends to have high precision and low recall.

selftest.q: AI 4 · What is a loss function, and what does gradient descent do with it?
selftest.a: A loss function is one number for how wrong the model's predictions are. Gradient descent works out which direction makes the loss go down fastest and nudges the weights a small step that way, again and again.

selftest.q: AI 5 · In one or two sentences, what does attention do inside a transformer?
selftest.a: Each token builds its new representation as a weighted mix of the other tokens' information. The weights come from how well its query matches their keys, so a word like "it" can pull meaning from the noun it refers to.

title: Python and Big-O · What machine learning is

blocks.title: Python for interviews: idioms, built-ins and Big-O
points: Big-O says how the work grows as the input grows. Drop constants and keep the biggest term: 2n + 5 is O(n).
A loop inside a loop over the same n items is O(n²). Sorting is O(n log n). One pass is O(n).
Space counts too: a new list or set of n items is O(n) extra space.
`x in some_list` scans the list: O(n). `x in some_set` or `key in some_dict` is O(1) on average, because it jumps straight to a hashed slot.
List costs: append and pop from the end are O(1). `pop(0)` and `insert(0, x)` shift every item, so they are O(n). Slicing `a[i:j]` copies the j − i items it takes: O(j − i).
Building a string with `+=` in a loop can copy it every time. Collect parts in a list and `''.join(parts)` once.
Use the built-ins: `enumerate` for index and value, `zip` to walk two lists together, and `sorted(items, key=...)` with a tuple key to sort by several things.
In an interview, say the Big-O of your plan before you code it, then again at the end.
blocks.say: Before coding I state the time and space Big-O, and I pick the container whose operations make that Big-O true: a set for membership, a list for order.
example: Task: do two lists, a with n items and b with m items, share any item?
Try 1: for each x in a, check `x in b`. Each check scans b, so n × m checks: O(n·m) time, O(1) extra space.
Try 2: put b in a set (O(m) to build), then check each x of a against the set in O(1). O(n + m) time, O(m) extra space.
Tweak: build the set from the shorter list, so the extra memory is O(min(n, m)).
Trade-off to say out loud: try 2 is much faster but uses memory; try 1 only wins when both lists are tiny or memory is very tight.

blocks.title: What machine learning is: features, labels, supervised vs unsupervised (k-means as the example)
points: Machine learning means learning a rule from examples instead of writing the rule by hand.
Features are the inputs, one column each: a flat's area, its floor, its distance to the metro. The label is the answer we want to predict: its rent.
Supervised learning trains on examples that come with labels. It predicts a number (regression, like rent) or a category (classification, like spam or not).
Unsupervised learning has no labels. It finds structure, such as groups of similar customers.
k-means is the classic unsupervised method. Pick k, place k centres, give each point to its nearest centre, move each centre to the average of its points, and repeat until nothing moves.
k-means needs k chosen up front, and a bad start can give a poor grouping, so it is often run a few times from different starts.
Always keep some labelled examples aside (a test set) to check the model on data it never saw.
blocks.say: Supervised learning learns from examples that carry the right answer; unsupervised learning finds structure without answers, like k-means grouping points around k centres.
example: Points on a line: 1, 2, 3, 10, 11, 12. Group them with k = 2, starting centres at 1 and 2.
Assign: 1 is nearest centre 1. 2, 3, 10, 11 and 12 are nearer centre 2.
Assign again: 1, 2 and 3 are nearer 1 than 7.6; 10, 11 and 12 are nearer 7.6.
Move: centre 1 = (1 + 2 + 3) / 3 = 2. Centre 2 = 11. Assign again: nothing changes, so stop.

selftest.q: What is the average cost of `x in a_list` compared with `x in a_set`, and why?
selftest.a: O(n) for the list, because it checks items one by one. O(1) on average for the set, because it hashes x and jumps straight to its slot.

selftest.q: What is a feature and what is a label?
selftest.a: A feature is an input the model sees, like a flat's area. The label is the answer it should predict, like the rent.

selftest.q: Why is supervised learning called supervised, and why is k-means unsupervised?
selftest.a: Supervised learning is trained with the right answers attached, like a teacher marking work. k-means gets no answers; it only groups points by distance.

selftest.q: You have a list of n words and must check m query words against it. What is the Big-O with the list, and with a set built from it?
selftest.a: List: O(n·m), since each query scans the list. Set: O(n) to build it, then O(1) per query, so O(n + m) in total.

selftest.q: Run k-means by hand on points 0, 1, 9, 10 with k = 2 and starting centres 0 and 1. Where do the centres end up?
selftest.a: Round 1: 0 goes to centre 0; 1, 9 and 10 go to centre 1, which moves to 20/3 ≈ 6.7. Round 2: 0 and 1 go to centre 0, 9 and 10 to the other. Centres become 0.5 and 9.5, and nothing changes after that.

title: Hashing and counting · Classes in Python

blocks.title: Arrays and hashing: dicts, sets, counting
blocks.builds_on: Day 1 · Big-O: a set or dict lookup is O(1) on average, a list scan is O(n)
points: A dict maps keys to values, with O(1) average get, set and `in`. A set is a dict with keys only.
Keys must be hashable, meaning they can't change: str, int and tuple work, but a list doesn't. Turn a list into a tuple to use it as a key.
Counting: `Counter(items)` counts everything in one O(n) pass. `counts[x] = counts.get(x, 0) + 1` is the same thing by hand.
Grouping: `defaultdict(list)` and `groups[key].append(item)`. The key is whatever the items in one group share.
The seen pattern: walk once, and for each item ask whether the item you need is already in the set or dict, before adding this one.
Most hashing answers trade O(n) extra memory for turning O(n²) into O(n). Say that trade out loud.
blocks.say: When I need fast lookups, counts or groups, I reach for a dict or a set: one O(n) pass with O(n) extra memory instead of O(n²) nested loops.
example: Task: find the first character that repeats in "interview".
Keep a set called seen. Walk the string once.
i: not seen, add. n: add. t: add. e: add. r: add.
v: add. i: already in seen, so return "i".
One pass with O(1) set checks gives O(n) time. The set holds at most one entry per distinct character, so O(n) space in general.

blocks.title: Classes and objects in Python: state, behaviour, dataclasses
blocks.builds_on: Day 1 · Python built-ins: today's classes wrap those lists, dicts and sets
points: A class is a blueprint. An object is one thing built from it, with its own data.
State is the data an object holds (its attributes). Behaviour is what it can do (its methods).
`__init__` sets the starting state. `self` is the object the method is running on.
Keep the rule next to the data: the method that changes state should check it, for example `withdraw` refuses to go below zero.
`@dataclass` writes `__init__`, `__repr__` and `__eq__` for you, which suits classes that mostly hold data.
`@dataclass(frozen=True)` makes objects that can't change after creation. Good for values like Money or a Ticket.
Machine-coding rounds score readable classes with clear names more than clever code.
blocks.say: An object bundles state with the behaviour that changes it, so the rules live in one place; I use dataclasses for plain data and normal classes when there are rules to guard.
example: Model a bank account: its state is owner and balance; its behaviour is deposit and withdraw.
class Account: __init__(self, owner) sets self.owner = owner and self.balance = 0.
deposit(self, amount): raise ValueError if amount <= 0, else add it to self.balance.
withdraw(self, amount): raise ValueError if amount > self.balance, else subtract it.
A record of each move is plain data: @dataclass(frozen=True) class Txn: kind: str, amount: int.
Now no caller can make the balance negative; the rule lives inside the class.

selftest.q: Why can't a list be a dict key, and what do you use instead?
selftest.a: A list can change, so its hash could change and the dict would lose it. Use a tuple, which can't change.

selftest.q: What does @dataclass write for you?
selftest.a: __init__ from the fields, a readable __repr__, and __eq__ that compares the fields. frozen=True also blocks changes after creation.

selftest.q: In the seen pattern, why do you check the set before adding the current item?
selftest.a: So an item never matches itself. You ask whether an earlier item is the partner, then record this one for later items.

selftest.q: Group email addresses by domain: "a@x.com", "b@y.com", "c@x.com". What is the dict key, what holds each group, and what is the Big-O?
selftest.a: The key is the part after the @ (email.split("@")[1]). A defaultdict(list) maps each domain to its addresses. One pass: O(n) time, O(n) space.

selftest.q: A Cart class stores items in a public list, and callers append to it directly. What goes wrong, and what do you change?
selftest.a: Nothing stops a caller adding a bad item or a negative quantity, and the rules end up spread across callers. Add add_item and remove_item methods that check the rules, and keep the list internal.

title: Two pointers and sliding window · Linear regression

blocks.title: Two pointers and sliding window
blocks.builds_on: Day 2 · counting with a dict, used today to track what is inside a window
points: Two pointers: keep two indexes and move them by a rule instead of trying every pair. Each step rules out options, so the walk is O(n).
Opposite ends: on sorted data, start one pointer at each end and move them inward.
Same direction: a slow pointer marks where to write and a fast one reads ahead, for in-place filtering.
Sliding window: a run of neighbouring items from left to right. Move right to grow it; move left to shrink it when it breaks the rule.
Keep a running total or a count dict for the window, so each move costs O(1) instead of re-adding the whole window.
Each index enters the window once and leaves once, so a sliding window is O(n) even though it has a loop inside a loop.

Fixed-size windows add one item and drop one. Variable windows shrink only while the rule is broken, which works when adding an item can never fix a broken window, for example a sum limit with all numbers ≥ 0.
blocks.say: Instead of checking every pair or every subarray, I move two indexes by a rule; each index moves forward at most n times, so it is O(n).
example: Task: longest run of 1s in [1, 1, 0, 1, 1, 1, 0, 1] if you may flip at most one 0.
Window rule: at most one 0 inside. Keep zeros = count of 0s in the window.
Move right one step at a time. Up to index 5 there is one 0, so the window is indices 0 to 5, length 6.
Index 6 is a second 0, so zeros = 2. Move left forward until zeros = 1: left passes the 0 at index 2 and stops at 3.
Window 3 to 6 (length 4), then 3 to 7 (length 5). The best stays 6.
Each index is added once and removed at most once, so the work is O(n).

blocks.title: Linear regression and the loss function
blocks.builds_on: Day 1 · supervised learning: features in, a labelled number out (regression)
points: Linear regression predicts a number with a straight line: prediction = w × x + b.
w (the weight) is the slope: how much the prediction moves when x goes up by 1. b (the bias) is where the line crosses x = 0.
With several features it is the same idea: w1 × x1 + w2 × x2 + … + b.
The error for one example is prediction minus the true label.
The loss is one number for how wrong the model is overall. Mean squared error (MSE) averages the squared errors.
Squaring stops positive and negative errors cancelling and punishes big misses more than small ones.
Training means finding the w and b that give the lowest loss. On Day 7 gradient descent does that search for us.
blocks.say: Linear regression fits prediction = w·x + b, and training picks w and b to minimise a loss such as mean squared error, the average squared gap between prediction and truth.
example: Guess w = 2, b = 0. Predictions 2, 4, 6. Errors 0, 0, 1. MSE = (0 + 0 + 1) / 3 ≈ 0.33.
MSE = (0.03 + 0.11 + 0.03) / 3 ≈ 0.06. A lower loss means a better line.
1.5 and 0.67 is in fact the best possible line for these three points.

selftest.q: Why is a sliding window O(n) even though it has a loop inside a loop?
selftest.a: The left index only moves forward, so across the whole run it moves at most n times. Each item enters once and leaves once.

selftest.q: What do w and b mean in prediction = w × x + b?
selftest.a: w is the slope: the change in prediction when x rises by 1. b is the bias: the prediction when x is 0.

selftest.q: Why square the errors in MSE instead of adding them as they are?
selftest.a: Plain errors can cancel (+3 and -3 add to 0) and hide a bad model. Squaring makes every error count and punishes big misses more.

selftest.q: Find the longest run of neighbouring numbers in [3, 1, 2, 1, 1, 4] whose sum is at most 5. Which pattern, and what is the answer?
selftest.a: A variable sliding window with a running sum: grow right, and while the sum is over 5 shrink from the left. This works because every number is ≥ 0. The answer is 4: [1, 2, 1, 1].

title: Stack, queue, linked list · A request's journey

blocks.title: Stack, queue and linked list
blocks.builds_on: Day 1 · list costs: append and pop at the end are O(1), pop(0) is O(n)
points: A stack is last in, first out, like a pile of plates. In Python: list.append to push and list.pop() to pop, both O(1).
Reach for a stack when the most recent unfinished thing matters: undo, matching brackets, going back.
A queue is first in, first out, like a ticket line. Use collections.deque: append and popleft are both O(1). A list's pop(0) is O(n).
A linked list is a chain of nodes, each holding a value and a pointer to the next node.
Inserting or removing next to a node you already hold is O(1). Finding the i-th node means walking from the head: O(n).
A dummy head (a fake node before the real first one) means you never special-case removing the first node.
Draw the pointers before you change them, and change them in an order that never loses the rest of the list.
blocks.say: A stack gives me the most recent item, a queue the oldest, and a linked list cheap inserts and removals where I already hold a node; I pick by which item I need next.
example: Browser history is a stack. Visit A, B, C: the stack is [A, B, C] and C is on screen.
Press back: pop C, and B is on screen. The stack is [A, B].
A print queue is a deque. Jobs j1 and j2 arrive: append both. The printer takes popleft(), which is j1, the oldest.
A playlist is a linked list: 1 → 2 → 3. To drop 2, point 1's next at 3. Nothing else moves.
With a dummy node d → 1 → 2 → 3, removing 1 is the same move: point d's next at 2.

blocks.title: A request's journey: DNS, TCP, HTTP, server, database
points: DNS turns a name like shop.example.com into an IP address. The answer is cached by the browser, the operating system and the resolver, so most lookups are fast.
TCP opens a reliable connection with a three-step handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK): one network round trip before any data moves.
For HTTPS, TLS then agrees on encryption keys, which adds about one more round trip.
An HTTP request has a method (GET, POST), a path, headers and an optional body. The response has a status code (200 OK, 404 not found, 500 server error), headers and a body.
The server runs your code. It often asks a database, which is another network hop plus the query time.
Every hop adds delay. Round trips across a network and slow database queries usually cost the most.
In a design interview, this journey is the skeleton you draw first: client, DNS, server, database.
blocks.say: A request resolves the name with DNS, opens a TCP connection and TLS on top, sends HTTP, and the server runs code that usually hits a database; each hop adds latency, so I know which ones dominate.
example: You open https://shop.example.com/products/42.
DNS: the browser asks the resolver for shop.example.com and gets 203.0.113.7.
TCP + TLS: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK, then the TLS handshake. About two round trips so far.
HTTP: GET /products/42 with headers such as Host and Cookie.
Server: the app looks up product 42 in the database, builds JSON and replies 200 OK.
Browser: reads the response and renders the page. Next time, DNS is cached and the connection can be reused.

selftest.q: Why use collections.deque instead of a list for a queue?
selftest.a: deque.popleft() is O(1). list.pop(0) shifts every other item left, so it is O(n).

selftest.q: What does DNS do, and why is it usually fast?
selftest.a: It turns a host name into an IP address. The answer is cached in the browser, the operating system and the resolver, so most requests skip the full lookup.

selftest.q: What does a dummy head node save you in linked-list code?
selftest.a: A special case for the first node. Every real node then has a node before it, so removing or inserting at the front is the same code as anywhere else.

selftest.q: A page loads slowly only on the first visit, and fast after. Name two hops that might explain it.
selftest.a: The first visit pays for the DNS lookup and the new TCP and TLS handshakes; later visits use the cached DNS answer and reuse the open connection. A cold server-side cache is another possibility.

selftest.q: Your text editor needs undo and redo. Which structure, and how do they work together?
selftest.a: Two stacks. Each edit pushes onto undo and clears redo. Undo pops from undo and pushes onto redo; redo does the reverse.

title: Binary search and recursion · Processes and threads

blocks.title: Binary search and recursion
blocks.builds_on: Day 4 · the stack: each recursive call waits on the call stack until the smaller call returns
points: Binary search needs sorted data. Look at the middle, then throw away the half that can't hold the answer. Halving each time makes it O(log n).
To find one value: keep lo and hi as the range still possible, loop while lo <= hi, with mid = (lo + hi) // 2. Python's bisect module does the sorted-list versions for you.
It also works on answers, not just arrays: if a yes/no check flips once, from no to yes, binary search finds where it flips.

To find the first index where a check turns true: lo, hi = 0, len(nums); while lo < hi, take mid; if the check holds at mid, hi = mid (mid might be the first), else lo = mid + 1. lo ends on the first true, or len(nums) if none.
Recursion means a function solves a smaller copy of the problem by calling itself.
Every recursive function needs a base case that returns without calling itself, or it never stops.
Each call waits on the call stack, so the extra space is O(depth). Python stops at about 1,000 levels.
blocks.say: Binary search halves the search space each step, so it is O(log n); recursion solves a smaller copy of the same problem, and I always state the base case first.
example: mid = 2, value 5. 5 < 7, so the answer is to the right: lo = 3.
mid = 4, value 9. 9 > 7, so go left: hi = 3.
mid = 3, value 7. Found at index 3 after three looks instead of up to six.
Recursion: total([1, 2, 3]) = 1 + total([2, 3]) = 1 + 2 + total([3]) = 1 + 2 + 3 + total([]). Each call waits on the stack.
The base case total([]) = 0 returns first. Then the waiting calls finish on the way back up: 3 + 0 = 3, then 2 + 3 = 5, then 1 + 5 = 6.

blocks.title: Processes vs threads, and context switches
blocks.builds_on: Day 4 · a request's journey: the server that runs your code is a process on a machine
points: A process is a running program with its own memory, files and at least one thread.
A thread is one line of execution inside a process. Threads of one process share its memory.
Shared memory makes threads cheap to start and quick to share data, but two threads changing the same data at once can corrupt it. Locks prevent that, and come later in the plan.
Processes are isolated: one crashing doesn't take down the others, but sharing data needs pipes, queues or a database.
A context switch is the operating system pausing one thread, saving where it was, and resuming another. It is pure overhead.
Switching between processes costs more than between threads, because the memory view changes too and the CPU's caches go cold.
In standard CPython, the GIL lets only one thread run Python code at a time. Threads help when waiting on network or disk; for heavy computing, use processes.
blocks.say: A process owns its memory and a thread is a path of execution inside it that shares that memory; in Python I use threads for waiting on I/O and processes for CPU-heavy work.
example: A web server must handle three slow downloads at once.
Option 1: one process with three threads. Cheap, and they share an in-memory cache, but one bad thread can crash all three.
Option 2: three processes. More memory and slower switches, but a crash stays contained.
The work is mostly waiting on the network, so in Python threads are fine: the GIL is released while a thread waits.

blocks.title: Trees and graphs: BFS and DFS
blocks.builds_on: Day 4 · stack and queue, and Day 5 · recursion: DFS is recursion or a stack, BFS is a queue
points: A tree is nodes joined by edges, with one root and no loops. A binary tree node has a value, a left child and a right child.
A graph is nodes and edges with no such limits: it can have loops and be split into parts. Store it as an adjacency list: a dict from each node to its neighbours.
DFS (depth-first) goes as deep as it can before backing up. Write it as recursion, or with an explicit stack.
BFS (breadth-first) visits level by level using a deque as a queue. In an unweighted graph it finds the fewest-edges path.
In a graph, keep a visited set and mark a node when you first reach it, or loops will trap you.
Both visit every node and edge once: O(V + E) time, where V is nodes and E is edges, and O(V) memory.
blocks.say: BFS uses a queue and explores level by level, so it finds the fewest-hops path; DFS uses recursion or a stack and goes deep first; both are O(V + E) with a visited set.
example: Graph: A–B, A–C, B–D, C–D, D–E. Find the fewest hops from A to E.
BFS: queue [A], visited {A}. Take A and add B and C: queue [B, C].
Take B: A is already visited, so add D. Queue [C, D].
Take C: A and D are already visited. Queue [D].
Take D and add E. Take E: it is the target. Levels A(0), B and C(1), D(2), E(3), so 3 hops.
DFS from A might go A, B, D, C, then E: it reaches everything but says nothing about the shortest path.

blocks.title: Scaling out: stateless servers behind a load balancer
blocks.builds_on: Day 4 · a request's journey: DNS gave one IP; now that IP belongs to a load balancer
points: Scaling up means a bigger machine. It is simple but has a ceiling, and that one machine is a single point of failure.
Scaling out means more machines running the same code. It needs something in front to share the requests: a load balancer.
Common ways to pick a server: round robin (take turns), least connections (the least busy), and hashing a user id (the same user always goes to the same server).
The load balancer runs health checks and stops sending traffic to a server that fails them.
Servers must be stateless: no login session in one server's memory. Put sessions in a shared store such as Redis, or in a signed token the client sends each time.
Sticky sessions (one user pinned to one server) are a workaround. They break when that server dies and make load uneven.
The load balancer is run as a redundant pair so it isn't the new single point of failure. The database becomes the next bottleneck, which later days cover.
blocks.say: I scale the web tier out by keeping servers stateless, with sessions in a shared store, and putting them behind a health-checked load balancer, so any server can take any request and I add capacity by adding machines.
example: Start: one server runs the app and keeps logged-in sessions in its memory. Traffic triples.
Add two more servers. A user logs in on server 1, but the next request lands on server 2 and they are logged out.
Fix: move sessions into Redis. Every server reads the session from there, so the servers are now stateless.
Put a load balancer in front, using least connections and a health check every few seconds.
Server 2 crashes: its health check fails, traffic goes to 1 and 3, and nobody is logged out.
Point DNS at the load balancer's address. The next weak spot is the single database.

selftest.q: Which traversal finds the fewest-hops path in an unweighted graph, and why?
selftest.a: BFS. It visits every node one hop away before any node two hops away, so the first time it reaches the target is by the fewest hops.

selftest.q: What does stateless mean for a web server, and why does it matter behind a load balancer?
selftest.a: The server keeps no per-user data in its own memory between requests. Then any server can handle any request, so the load balancer can spread traffic and drop a dead server freely.

selftest.q: Why does graph BFS or DFS need a visited set when tree traversal does not?
selftest.a: Graphs can have loops, so without it you revisit nodes forever. A tree has no loops, so each node is reached exactly once.

selftest.q: Your app keeps a shopping cart in server memory, and you go from 1 to 4 servers. What breaks, and what are two fixes?

selftest.q: A maze is a grid of open cells and walls. You move up, down, left or right. How do you find the fewest moves from the top-left to the bottom-right?
selftest.a: Treat each open cell as a node joined to its open neighbours, and run BFS from the start with a visited set. The level at which BFS first reaches the exit is the fewest moves. O(rows × cols).

blocks.title: Heaps, and a first feel for dynamic programming
blocks.builds_on: Day 6 · trees (a heap is a tree kept in a list) and Day 5 · recursion (dynamic programming is recursion that remembers)
points: A heap always keeps the smallest item at the front. Python's heapq stores it in a plain list, so heap[0] is the smallest.
The list is a binary tree read level by level: the children of index i sit at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, and every parent is ≤ its children.
heappush and heappop are O(log n). heapify turns a list into a heap in O(n).
heapq is a min-heap only. For a max-heap, push negated numbers.
k largest: keep a min-heap of size k and pop the smallest when it grows past k. That is O(n log k), better than sorting when k is small.
Dynamic programming (DP) fits when plain recursion solves the same smaller problem again and again.
Memoise: store each answer the first time and reuse it. functools.cache does this for a function in one line.
Three questions set up any DP: what is the state (the inputs that define a subproblem), what choice do I make, and what is the base case?
blocks.say: A heap gives me the smallest item in O(1) and push or pop in O(log n), which makes top-k O(n log k); dynamic programming is recursion that stores answers to repeated subproblems.
example: Heap: the 3 largest of [5, 1, 9, 3, 7, 2], with a min-heap capped at 3. heappush 5, 1, 9: heap [1, 5, 9], so heap[0] = 1.
heappush 3 → size 4, so heappop removes 1: [3, 5, 9]. heappush 7 → heappop removes 3: [5, 7, 9].
heappush 2 → heappop removes 2 itself: [5, 7, 9]. The heap holds the top 3: 5, 7 and 9.
DP: fib(n) = fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2), fib(0) = 0, fib(1) = 1. Plain recursion for fib(5) calls fib(3) twice and fib(2) three times, and the repeats grow exponentially.
Add @functools.cache: the second fib(3) is just a lookup, so each n from 0 to 5 is computed once: O(n) time and memory.
Bottom-up: a, b = 0, 1, then a, b = b, a + b, n times. O(1) memory.

blocks.title: The four OOP ideas in Python, and composition over inheritance
blocks.builds_on: Day 2 · classes and objects: state, behaviour and rules kept inside the class
points: Encapsulation: keep data and the rules that guard it together, and let callers use methods. In Python, a leading underscore marks something as internal.
Abstraction: show what an object does and hide how. A caller asks pay(amount) and doesn't care whether it is UPI or a card.
Inheritance: a subclass is a kind of its parent and reuses its code, as in class Car(Vehicle).
Polymorphism: the same call does the right thing for each type. shape.area() works for a circle and a square alike.
An abstract base class (abc.ABC with @abstractmethod) declares the methods every subclass must provide.
Composition: an object has parts and passes work to them, as in Logger(sink, formatter). Parts can be swapped without touching the Logger.
Prefer composition. Inheritance ties a subclass to its parent's insides, and mixing two kinds of variation by inheritance multiplies classes: 2 sinks × 2 formats = 4 subclasses.
blocks.say: I use inheritance only for a true is-a relationship with a shared interface, and otherwise compose objects from small swappable parts, which keeps classes few and testable.
example: Need: send notices by email or SMS, in plain or HTML format.
With inheritance: PlainEmail, HtmlEmail, PlainSms, HtmlSms. A third channel makes six classes.
With composition: Notifier(channel, formatter). channel has send(to, text); formatter has format(msg).
Notifier.notify(to, msg) calls channel.send(to, formatter.format(msg)).

blocks.title: Gradient descent: walking downhill on the loss
blocks.builds_on: Day 3 · linear regression and MSE: the loss we now minimise automatically
points: Goal: find the w and b with the lowest loss without guessing by hand.
The gradient is the slope of the loss for each parameter. It points uphill, so step the other way.
Update rule: w = w - learning_rate × (slope of the loss with respect to w), and the same for b.
For MSE with prediction = w × x + b, the slope for w is the average of 2 × error × x, and for b the average of 2 × error.
The learning rate is the step size. Too big and the loss jumps around or grows; too small and training crawls.
Repeat until the loss stops dropping. Each full pass over the data is called an epoch.
On big data, each step uses a small random batch instead of every example: stochastic or mini-batch gradient descent.
blocks.say: Gradient descent computes how the loss changes with each weight and steps every weight a little in the downhill direction, with the learning rate setting the step size.
example: Day 3 data (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 5). Start at w = 0, b = 0, learning rate 0.1. MSE = 15.
Predictions 0, 0, 0, so errors (prediction - truth) are -2, -4, -5.
Slope for w = average of 2 × error × x = 2 × (-2 - 8 - 15) / 3 ≈ -16.7. Slope for b = 2 × (-11) / 3 ≈ -7.3.
New MSE ≈ 0.23, down from 15 in one step. Many more steps settle near w = 1.5, b = 0.67.

blocks.title: Logistic regression and cross-entropy loss
blocks.builds_on: Day 3 · linear regression and MSE, and Day 7 · gradient descent: today swaps in a new output and a new loss
points: Logistic regression predicts a yes/no label, which is called classification: spam or not, will the user click or not.
It starts like linear regression: z = w × x + b. Then the sigmoid, σ(z) = 1 / (1 + e^(−z)), squashes z into a probability between 0 and 1.
σ(0) = 0.5. A large positive z gives nearly 1, and a large negative z nearly 0.
To decide, compare the probability with a threshold, usually 0.5. Moving it trades catching more positives against more false alarms; Day 21 covers choosing it.
The loss is binary cross-entropy, also called log loss. For one example it is −log(p) when the label is 1 and −log(1 − p) when it is 0, averaged over all examples.
It punishes confident mistakes hard: p = 0.99 on a true 0 costs about 4.6, while p = 0.6 on a true 0 costs about 0.9.
Why not MSE: with the sigmoid, MSE makes a bumpy loss with flat stretches where gradient descent stalls. Log loss gives one smooth bowl.
Gradient descent (Day 7) works unchanged. The slope for w is the average of (p − y) × x, and for b the average of (p − y).
blocks.say: Logistic regression puts w·x + b through a sigmoid to get a probability, and trains by minimising log loss, which punishes confident wrong answers far more than unsure ones.
example: A spam filter with one feature, x = how many times "FREE!!" appears, and w = 1.5, b = −3.
x = 4: z = 1.5 × 4 − 3 = 3, so p = σ(3) ≈ 0.95. That is above 0.5, so: spam.
x = 1: z = −1.5, so p ≈ 0.18: not spam. x = 2: z = 0, so p = 0.5, right on the line.
If the x = 4 email really is spam (y = 1), its loss is −ln 0.95 ≈ 0.05. If it is not (y = 0), the loss is −ln 0.05 ≈ 3.0.
In that second case p − y = 0.95, so the slope for w is 0.95 × 4 ≈ 3.8. Gradient descent lowers w, and the next prediction is less confident.

blocks.title: Arrays & Hashing: a dict that remembers counts and indexes
blocks.builds_on: Day 2 · Counter and the seen set, and Day 8 · the problem routine
points: Day 2's seen set stored only "have I seen it?". Today the dict stores something you will need later: a count, or the index where you saw a value.
Counting to compare: a Counter (or a dict of counts) summarises what a string holds and ignores the order. Two Counters compare with == in O(n).

Complement lookup: when a pair must meet a rule, work out the partner each item needs and ask the dict whether that partner has already passed. Check before you store, so an item never pairs with itself.
When the answer needs positions, store the index as the dict's value: seen[value] = i.

Not every array problem needs a dict. To compare several strings position by position, check index i in each one, and i can't pass the end of the shortest. `zip(*words)` groups the i-th characters of all words and stops at the shortest.
Slicing copies: s[:i] costs O(i). Take a slice once at the end, not inside a loop.
Edge cases today: empty strings, a single word, strings of different lengths, and a value that appears twice.
blocks.say: I keep a dict of what I've already passed, a count or an index, so each item asks one O(1) question instead of scanning the rest: O(n) time for O(n) memory.
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): in [10, 2, 5, 3], find the positions of a number and its double.
seen = {} maps value → index. i = 0, x = 10: is its double 20 or its half 5 in seen? No. Store seen[10] = 0.
i = 1, x = 2: is 4 or 1 in seen? No. Store seen[2] = 1.
i = 2, x = 5: is its double 10 in seen? Yes, at index 0. Return (0, 2), because 10 is double 5.
One pass with one O(1) dict check per item: O(n) time and O(n) memory, instead of O(n²) for checking every pair.

blocks.title: SOLID 1: single responsibility and open/closed
blocks.builds_on: Day 7 · composition and abstract base classes: SOLID says when to split a class and how to extend it
points: SOLID is five rules for classes that stay easy to change. Today: S and O.
Single responsibility: a class should have one reason to change, meaning one job that one group of people asks you to change.
Smell: a name with "And" or "Manager", or one class that computes, formats and saves. Each part changes for a different reason, so every edit risks the others.
Fix: split it into small classes with one job each, and let a coordinator use them (composition, Day 7).
Open/closed: add new behaviour by adding code, not by editing code that already works and is tested.
Smell: an if/elif chain on a type string ('student', 'staff', …) that grows with every new case and is often copied into several methods.
Fix: one class per case behind a shared abstract method, plus a dict from name to object. A new case is one new class and one dict entry. Day 16's Strategy pattern builds on exactly this.
Don't split or abstract before a second reason or a second case actually shows up. An interface with a single implementation is just more code to read.
blocks.say: A class should have one reason to change, and new cases should arrive as new classes rather than new elif branches; I apply both once a second reason or case actually shows up.
example: Start: an Invoice class with total(), to_pdf() and email(). It has three reasons to change: tax rules, the PDF layout and the mail provider.
Single responsibility: split it into InvoiceCalculator.total(items), PdfRenderer.render(invoice) and Mailer.send(to, file). InvoiceService holds all three and calls them in order.
The discount code reads: if kind == "student": 10% off, elif kind == "staff": 20% off. A festival discount means editing this tested method.
Open/closed: an abstract Discount class with apply(total), implemented by StudentDiscount and StaffDiscount. DISCOUNTS = {"student": StudentDiscount(), "staff": StaffDiscount()}.
Adding FestivalDiscount is one new class and one dict entry. Nothing that already works is edited.

selftest.q: In a complement lookup, why do you check the dict before storing the current item?
selftest.a: So an item never pairs with itself. You ask whether an earlier item is the partner, and only then record this one for later items.

selftest.q: What does the single responsibility principle say, and what is one sign a class breaks it?

selftest.a: Adding a new case shouldn't mean editing working code. Put each case in its own class behind a shared abstract method, look them up in a dict, and add new cases as new classes.

blocks.title: Arrays & Hashing: inside a hash set (buckets and collisions)
blocks.builds_on: Day 3 · same-direction pointers for in-place filtering, and Day 9 · a dict that keeps counts
points: In-place filtering (Day 3): a write index marks where the next kept item goes, and a read loop visits every item. O(n) time and O(1) extra memory; the judge reads only the first k slots.

Counting (Day 2) answers "which value appears most?" in O(n) time and O(n) memory. If a follow-up asks for O(1) memory, try it after your first version passes, and watch the video for the idea if stuck.
Today's new idea: a hash set is a list of buckets. hash(key) % number_of_buckets picks the bucket, so you only ever search that one bucket.
Two keys in one bucket is a collision. Chaining keeps a small list in each bucket: add appends the key if it isn't there, remove deletes it, and contains scans only that list.
Load factor = keys ÷ buckets. When it passes a limit such as 0.75, double the buckets and re-insert every key (rehashing). One resize costs O(n) but happens rarely, so add stays O(1) on average.
Average O(1) needs short buckets. If every key landed in one bucket, every operation would be O(n), so say both the average and the worst case.
Design problems: write the class with exactly the methods asked, test each one on a tiny case, and state the Big-O of each method.
blocks.say: A hash set hashes each key to one bucket and chains collisions in a short list; keeping the load factor low by resizing keeps add, remove and contains at O(1) on average, O(n) in the worst case.
example: A set of roll numbers with 4 buckets, where bucket = roll % 4. Start: [[], [], [], []].
add 10 → 10 % 4 = 2. add 7 → bucket 3. add 14 → bucket 2 again: a collision, so bucket 2 is [10, 14].
contains 14 → go to bucket 2 and scan [10, 14]: found after two checks, without looking at any other bucket.
remove 10 → bucket 2 is [14]. add 3 and then 21: the buckets are [[], [21], [14], [7, 3]].
4 keys ÷ 4 buckets = load 1.0, over 0.75. Grow to 8 buckets and re-insert: 14 → 6, 7 → 7, 3 → 3, 21 → 5. Every bucket now holds at most one key.

blocks.title: Train, validation and test sets, and data leakage
blocks.builds_on: Day 1 · keep labelled examples aside for testing, and Day 8 · logistic regression and its threshold
points: Training set: the model learns its weights from it. Validation set: you compare models and choose settings on it, such as Day 8's threshold. Test set: used once, at the end, for the honest score.
Typical splits are 70/15/15 or 80/10/10. Stratify, so each label's share is the same in every split; that matters most when a label is rare.
Keep the test set apart from validation: every choice you make by looking at validation scores fits the model a little to that set, so its score drifts too high.

Split first. Anything that learns from data is fitted on the training rows only, then applied to validation and test. Scaling (StandardScaler) is the usual case: it subtracts each feature's mean and divides by its spread, so features on very different ranges, such as income and age, become comparable. Take that mean and spread from the training rows only.
Data leakage: information the model won't have at prediction time gets into training. Offline scores look great; real ones don't.
Common leaks: a feature recorded after the outcome, copies of the same user or item on both sides of the split, and a random split of time-ordered data, which trains on the future.
For time-ordered data, train on the past and test on later rows. When one user has many rows, keep all of that user's rows on one side.
A score that looks too good is a reason to hunt for a leak, not to celebrate.
blocks.say: I train on one set, choose settings on a validation set and report once on an untouched test set, splitting before any preprocessing so nothing from validation or test leaks into training.
example: Predict loan default from 10,000 past loans, 5% of which defaulted.
Split first, stratified: 7,000 train, 1,500 validation and 1,500 test, each with about 5% defaults (350, 75 and 75).
Scale income with the mean and spread of the 7,000 training rows only, and apply those same numbers to validation and test.
A feature days_in_collections gives near-perfect validation scores. It only exists after a default, so it is a leak: drop it.
Choose the threshold on validation (say 0.3 beats 0.5), then score the test set once and report that number.

selftest.q: In a hash set, what is a bucket, what is a collision, and how does chaining handle it?
selftest.a: A bucket is one slot in the list, chosen by hash(key) % number_of_buckets. A collision is two keys landing in the same bucket. Chaining keeps a small list in each bucket and scans only that list.

selftest.q: What is each of the training, validation and test sets for?
selftest.a: Training: the model learns its weights. Validation: you compare models and choose settings such as the threshold. Test: used once at the end for an honest score.

selftest.q: Why fit the scaler on the training rows only, not on all the data?
selftest.a: Otherwise the mean and spread include validation and test rows, so information from them leaks into training and the scores come out too optimistic.

selftest.q: Your hash set has 8 buckets and now holds 20 keys, and contains has got slow. Why, and what do you do?
selftest.a: The load factor is 2.5, so chains average 2 to 3 keys and some are longer. Grow to, say, 32 buckets and re-insert every key, then keep resizing whenever the load passes about 0.75.

selftest.q: A churn model scores 0.99 on validation. One feature is days_since_cancellation. What happened, and what do you do?

blocks.title: Arrays & Hashing: merge sort (divide and conquer), and keys for hash maps
blocks.builds_on: Day 10 · the bucket hash set (today adds values), Day 2 · grouping with defaultdict, and Day 5 · recursion with a base case
points: A hash map is yesterday's hash set with values: each bucket holds [key, value] pairs. put must update the value when the key is already there, not add a second pair.
Grouping (Day 2) is groups[key].append(item). The whole skill is the key: the same for items that belong together, different otherwise, and hashable (a str or a tuple, not a list).
Today's new idea, merge sort: split the list in half, sort each half by calling yourself, then merge the two sorted halves.
Base case (Day 5): a list of 0 or 1 items is already sorted, so return it as it is.
Merge: keep one index per half, append the smaller front item and move that index on. When one half runs out, append the rest of the other. O(n) for n items.
The list halves log n times, and each level merges n items in total, so merge sort is O(n log n) time in every case, with O(n) extra memory.
Slicing nums[:mid] copies mid items. That is O(n) per level, which the merge already pays, so the total stays O(n log n).
blocks.say: Merge sort splits the list, sorts each half recursively and merges them in O(n); log n levels of O(n) work give O(n log n) every time, using O(n) extra memory.
example: Sort the marks [38, 27, 43, 3].
Split into [38, 27] and [43, 3], then into single items, which are already sorted (the base case).
Merge [38] and [27] into [27, 38]. Merge [43] and [3] into [3, 43].
Merge [27, 38] with [3, 43]: 27 vs 3, take 3. 27 vs 43, take 27. 38 vs 43, take 38. The left half is empty, so append 43: [3, 27, 38, 43].
Two levels of merging, 4 items each: n × log n = 4 × 2 steps of work. Taking from the left half on a tie keeps equal items in their original order, which makes it a stable sort.

blocks.title: Back-of-the-envelope maths: requests per second, storage, bandwidth
blocks.builds_on: Day 6 · scaling out: estimates tell you how many servers you need and whether one database is enough
points: Estimates decide the design: one database or several, whether a cache is needed, how many servers. Within 10× is good enough, as long as you say every assumption out loud.
A day has 86,400 seconds; round it to 100,000 for mental maths. So 1 million requests a day is about 10 to 12 per second.
Requests per second (QPS) = daily active users × actions per user per day ÷ 86,400. Peak is often 2 to 3 times the average; say which multiplier you use.
Storage = new items per day × bytes per item × days kept × copies (often 3 replicas).
Bandwidth = QPS × bytes per request or response. Multiply bytes by 8 to get bits per second.
Sizes: KB = 10^3, MB = 10^6, GB = 10^9, TB = 10^12, PB = 10^15 bytes. One ASCII character is 1 byte, a 64-bit integer 8 bytes, and a phone photo a few hundred KB to a few MB.
Work out reads and writes separately. Many more reads than writes points to caching, which starts on Day 13.
Servers needed ≈ peak QPS ÷ what one server handles (assume, say, 1,000 simple requests per second), plus spare for failures.
blocks.say: I estimate QPS as users × actions ÷ 86,400 with a peak multiplier, storage as items × size × retention × replicas, and bandwidth as QPS × payload, rounding hard and stating each assumption.
example: Order history for a food-delivery app: 10 million daily users, each placing 0.2 orders and opening their history 5 times a day.
Writes: 2 million orders a day ÷ 86,400 ≈ 23 per second (the 100,000 shortcut says 20). Peak at 3× ≈ 70 per second.
Reads: 50 million history views a day ≈ 580 per second, peaking near 1,700. Reads outnumber writes 25 to 1.
Storage: 2 million orders × 1 KB = 2 GB a day, about 730 GB a year, or about 2.2 TB a year with 3 replicas.
Bandwidth: 1,700 peak reads × 10 KB per history page ≈ 17 MB/s, about 140 Mbit/s.
Verdict: storage fits one database; the read load is what to plan for, so a cache in front is worth it.

selftest.q: What is merge sort's time and extra memory, and why that time?
selftest.a: O(n log n) time in every case and O(n) extra memory. The list halves log n times, and merging at each level touches all n items.

selftest.q: Roughly how many seconds are in a day, and about how many requests per second is 1 million requests a day?

selftest.q: In a hash map, what goes wrong if put always appends a new [key, value] pair without checking for the key?

selftest.q: A photo app gets 2 million uploads a day at 500 KB each, kept 3 years with 3 copies. About how much storage is that?

selftest.q: Group words that use the same set of letters, ignoring how often each appears ("aab" goes with "ab" and "ba"). What is the key, and what is the Big-O?

Then today's pattern, counting sort: when values come from a small known set (three colours, five grades), count each value in one pass, then write them back in order in a second pass.
That is O(n + k) time for n items and k possible values, with O(k) memory. It beats O(n log n) because it never compares two items, but it only works when k is small and known.
"In place" means overwriting the given list slot by slot and returning nothing new.
If time is left, read the problem's one-pass follow-up and try it; otherwise leave it for the weekend.
blocks.say: When values come from a small fixed set, I count each value and rewrite the list in order: O(n + k) with no comparisons, instead of an O(n log n) sort.
example: Sort T-shirt orders ["L", "S", "M", "S", "L", "M", "S"] into S, M, L order, in place.
Pass 1, count: S 3, M 2, L 2.
Pass 2, rewrite: slots 0 to 2 get "S", slots 3 and 4 get "M", slots 5 and 6 get "L".
Result: ["S", "S", "S", "M", "M", "L", "L"]. Two passes and no comparisons between items: O(n + k) with k = 3.
The same idea fails for any number up to a billion: k would be huge, so use a normal O(n log n) sort there.

blocks.title: CPU scheduling basics: FCFS, round robin, priority
blocks.builds_on: Day 5 · processes, threads and context switches: the scheduler decides which thread runs next
points: The scheduler picks which ready thread runs next on each CPU core. Every switch is a context switch (Day 5), which costs time.
Measures: waiting time (ready but not running), turnaround time (finish minus arrival) and response time (first run minus arrival).
First come, first served (FCFS): run jobs in arrival order, each to the end. Simple, but one long job at the front makes every short job behind it wait. That is the convoy effect.
Shortest job first gives the lowest average waiting time, but the scheduler rarely knows how long a job will take.

Round robin: each job runs for a fixed time slice (the quantum), then goes to the back of the queue. Good response time for interactive work. Too small a quantum wastes time on switches; too large, and it behaves like FCFS.

Priority: the highest-priority ready job runs first, and in the preemptive version it interrupts a lower one. Low-priority jobs may then never run (starvation). The fix is aging: raise a job's priority the longer it waits.
Real systems mix these. Linux gives each thread a fair share of CPU time, weighted by its priority (its nice value).
blocks.say: FCFS is simple but short jobs queue behind long ones; round robin time-slices for good response at the cost of more context switches; priority scheduling needs aging so low-priority work doesn't starve.
example: Three jobs arrive at time 0 in the order A, B, C, needing 6, 2 and 1 ms of CPU.
FCFS: A runs 0–6, B 6–8, C 8–9. Waiting times 0, 6 and 8: an average of about 4.7 ms. The short jobs sat behind the long one.
Shortest first, for contrast: C 0–1, B 1–3, A 3–9. Waiting 0, 1 and 3: an average of about 1.3 ms, the best possible, but only if you know the lengths.
Round robin with a 2 ms quantum: A 0–2, B 2–4 (done), C 4–5 (done), A 5–9. Waiting A 3, B 2, C 4: an average of 3 ms, and every job starts within 4 ms.

Priority: if C handles a keypress and has top priority, it runs first, at 0–1, wherever it sits in the line. A steady stream of top-priority jobs could keep A waiting for ever, unless aging lifts A's priority.

selftest.a: When the values come from a small, known set of k values. It costs O(n + k) time and O(k) memory, because it counts and rewrites instead of comparing items.

points: Many problems are two steps: count with a dict (Day 2), then pick by count.

Picking with buckets: a count can never be more than n, so make a list of n + 1 buckets and put each item in bucket[its count].
Walking the buckets from the highest index down visits items most frequent first. Counting, filling and walking are each O(n), so O(n) in total, with no sort.
This turns Day 12's counting sort around: there the value picked the slot, here the count picks the slot.
Ties: if two items share a count, either order is usually fine. Ask the interviewer rather than guess.
blocks.say: I count with a dict, then pick by count: a size-k heap gives O(n log k), and buckets indexed by count give O(n), because a count can't be larger than n.

Walk from 6 down to 1 and write each letter count times: "aaa" + "nn" + "b" = "aaannb".
O(n) to count, O(distinct letters) to fill the buckets and O(n) to walk: O(n) overall, with no sort.

blocks.title: Caching: cache-aside, write-through, TTL, eviction, hit rate
blocks.builds_on: Day 11 · read-heavy estimates, and Day 6 · scaling out, where the single database became the next bottleneck
points: A cache keeps copies of often-read data in memory, for example in Redis, so most reads skip the database. A Redis read takes about a millisecond; a database query often takes several to tens.
Hit rate = hits ÷ all reads. At a 90% hit rate, the database sees only one read in ten.
Cache-aside, the usual default: read the cache; on a miss, read the database, store the result in the cache with a TTL, and return it. On a write, update the database, then delete the cached key.

Write-through: every write updates the cache and the database together, so the cache is always fresh, but writes are slower and you may cache data nobody reads. Write-back: write to the cache now and the database later, which is fast but loses data if the cache dies first.
TTL (time to live): each entry expires after a set time, which caps how stale it can get. Pick it by how much staleness is acceptable: minutes for a profile, seconds for a price.

Eviction: when memory is full, something must go. LRU drops the least recently used entry; LFU drops the least often used. LRU is the usual choice; in Redis you set it (allkeys-lru), since the default (noeviction) is to refuse writes when full.

Stampede: a hot key expires, and thousands of requests miss at once and all hit the database. Fixes: let one request refill the key while the rest wait, and add a little randomness (jitter) to TTLs so keys don't all expire together.
In an interview, say what you cache, the pattern, the TTL, the eviction policy and the hit rate you expect.
blocks.say: I put a cache-aside layer in front of the database for hot reads, with a TTL to bound staleness and LRU eviction, and size the win by the hit rate: at 95%, the database sees one read in twenty.
example: A product page gets 1,000 reads a second. A database query takes 20 ms; a Redis read takes 1 ms.
Cache-aside: a read for product 42 checks the key product:42. The first read misses, fetches from the database, and stores the result with a 10-minute TTL.
At a 95% hit rate, the database sees 50 reads a second instead of 1,000.
Average latency ≈ 0.95 × 1 ms + 0.05 × (1 + 20) ms ≈ 2 ms, against 20 ms with no cache.
A seller changes the price: update the database, then delete product:42, so the next read loads the new price. If the delete is lost, the TTL still caps staleness at 10 minutes.
Memory fills during a sale: LRU evicts products nobody has opened lately, and the popular ones stay.

selftest.q: In cache-aside, what happens on a read, and what happens on a write?
selftest.a: Read: check the cache; on a miss, read the database, store the value with a TTL and return it. Write: update the database, then delete the cached key so the next read reloads it.

selftest.q: What is the difference between a TTL and an eviction policy?
selftest.a: A TTL expires an entry after a set time, to cap staleness. Eviction removes entries when memory is full, to make room, choosing which ones by a rule such as LRU.

selftest.q: Why can an item's count be used as an index into a list of buckets?
selftest.a: In a list of n items, no count can be larger than n, so a list of n + 1 buckets has a slot for every possible count.

selftest.q: A service gets 2,000 reads a second with an 80% cache hit rate. How many reach the database, and what hit rate would halve that?
selftest.a: 20% of 2,000 = 400 a second. Halving it to 200 means a 10% miss rate, so a 90% hit rate.

selftest.q: Every day at noon a popular key expires and the database spikes for a few seconds. What is happening, and what are two fixes?
selftest.a: A cache stampede: many requests miss at once and all query the database. Fixes: let one request refill the key while the others wait, and add random jitter to TTLs (or refresh hot keys before they expire).

blocks.title: Arrays & Hashing: packing strings with a length header
blocks.builds_on: Day 1 · ''.join and slicing costs, and Day 9 · walking a string by index
points: The problem shape: pack a list of strings into one string, then get exactly the same list back. Every network message and file format has to solve this.
A plain separator breaks when the separator can appear inside the data: joining "a,b" and "c" with "," gives "a,b,c", which reads back as three strings.
Fix 1, escaping: mark every separator inside the data, as CSV does with quotes. It works, but both sides must handle the escapes carefully.
Fix 2, a length header: write each string's length, a marker, then the string. The reader reads the number up to the marker, then takes exactly that many characters, so the content can hold anything.
Lengths can have several digits (12, 105), so read digits until you reach the marker; never assume one digit.
Build the output as a list of parts and ''.join it once (Day 1), and slice each string once. Both directions are then O(total length).
Edge cases: an empty list, empty strings, and strings that contain the marker or digits.
blocks.say: Separators break when the data can contain them, so I put a length header before each string; the reader takes exactly that many characters and never has to look inside the data.
example: A chat client receives "5:hello12:how are you?0:" and must split it into messages.
i = 0: read digits up to ':' and get 5. Take the next 5 characters, "hello". i moves past them, to 7.
Read digits up to ':' and get 12 (two digits). Take the next 12 characters, "how are you?"; the spaces and the '?' don't matter.
Read 0: an empty message, "". i reaches the end, giving ["hello", "how are you?", ""].
With "|" as a separator instead, a message containing "|" would split in two. The length header never looks inside a message.

blocks.title: SOLID 2: Liskov, interface segregation, dependency inversion
blocks.builds_on: Day 9 · single responsibility and open/closed, and Day 7 · abstract base classes and composition
points: Liskov substitution: an object of a subclass must work anywhere its parent is expected. It accepts what the parent accepts and keeps the parent's promises.
The classic break is Square(Rectangle). Setting a square's width also changes its height, so code that sets width 5 and height 4 and expects area 20 gets 16.
Smell: a subclass method that raises NotImplementedError or quietly does nothing, like Day 7's RubberDuck. The parent promised something the child can't do.
Interface segregation: several small interfaces beat one big one, so no class has to write methods it doesn't need.
In Python, a small interface is an abc.ABC with one or two abstract methods, or a typing.Protocol: any class with the right methods fits, with no inheritance needed.

Dependency inversion: high-level code (the business rule) depends on an abstraction, and the concrete class (a database, an email provider) is passed in from outside. Passing it in is called dependency injection.
The payoff: tests pass in a fake, such as an in-memory store or a mailer that records messages, and swapping the database never touches the business rule.
blocks.say: Subclasses must keep their parent's promises, interfaces stay small, and business code depends on abstractions that are passed in, which is what makes it testable and swappable.
example: A Storage ABC has read(), write() and delete(). ArchiveStorage is read-only, so its write() raises an error, and code that writes to "any Storage" crashes on an archive. That breaks Liskov.
Split the interface: Reader has read(); Writer has write() and delete(). ArchiveStorage implements only Reader, and DiskStorage implements both.
ReportService only reads, so it asks for a Reader in __init__ instead of creating DiskStorage itself. That is dependency inversion.
In production: ReportService(DiskStorage("/data")). In a test: ReportService(FakeReader({"q3.csv": "1,2,3"})).
No subclass breaks a promise now, and the service can be tested without touching the disk.

blocks.title: Overfitting vs underfitting: bias and variance
blocks.builds_on: Day 10 · training and validation sets: comparing their errors is how you spot over- and underfitting
points: Underfitting: the model is too simple for the pattern, so it is wrong on training and validation data alike. This is high bias.
Overfitting: the model learns the training data's noise as if it were pattern, giving a low training error and a much higher validation error. This is high variance.
Bias is error from assumptions that are too simple, like fitting a straight line to a curve. Variance is how much the model would change if trained on a different sample of the data.
Diagnose with Day 10's split: both errors high means underfit; training low but validation far higher means overfit; both low and close means a good fit.
As a model gets more complex, bias falls and variance rises. Pick the complexity with the lowest validation error, not the lowest training error.
Fixes for underfitting: more or better features, a more flexible model, or training longer.
Fixes for overfitting: more training data, a simpler model or fewer features. Tomorrow (Day 15) adds regularisation and early stopping.
blocks.say: Underfitting is high error everywhere (bias); overfitting is low training error but high validation error (variance); I compare the two errors to tell which, and pick the complexity with the best validation error.
example: Data: 20 training points from y = sin(x) plus noise, and 100 validation points. Fit polynomials of three degrees with numpy.polyfit (degree d is Day 3's linear regression on the features x, x², …, x^d, so a higher degree is a more flexible model) (one run, seed 5).
Degree 1, a straight line: training MSE 0.24, validation 0.38. Both high: underfit.
Degree 3: training 0.04, validation 0.13. Both low: a good fit.
Degree 12: training 0.03, validation 0.95. The best training score and the worst validation score: overfit.
Degree 12 again with 200 more training points: training 0.09, validation 0.11. More data closes the gap.

title: Prefix sums · Regularisation

blocks.title: Arrays & Hashing: prefix sums, and passes from both ends
blocks.builds_on: Day 3 · a running sum for a fixed window, and Day 8 · building a new list with [0] * size
points: This week brings the topic's mediums (Days 15 to 18). From now on the points give the pattern and leave each problem's own move to you. The Day 8 routine stays the same.
Prefix sums: prefix[i] is the total of the first i items. Start with prefix[0] = 0, then prefix[i + 1] = prefix[i] + nums[i]. Building it is one O(n) pass.
The sum of nums[l..r] is then prefix[r + 1] − prefix[l]: O(1) per question, however long the range. It pays off when the data stays fixed and many ranges are asked.
The extra 0 at the front means a range that starts at index 0 needs no special case.

The idea extends to a grid: let each cell hold the total of the rectangle from the top-left corner down to it. Draw a 3 × 3 grid and work out which corner rectangles to add and subtract for any smaller rectangle.

Some questions need what is on both sides of index i. Make one pass from the left and one from the right, each carrying a running value, then combine them at i. Two O(n) passes beat re-scanning both sides for every i, which is O(n²).
Sums aren't the only thing you can carry: a running maximum, a count or any other value works the same way.
Edge cases: a range of one item, negative numbers (fine here, unlike Day 3's shrinking window), and zeros.
blocks.say: When the data is fixed and many ranges are asked, I build prefix sums once in O(n) so each range is one subtraction; when an answer needs both sides of i, I make one pass from the left and one from the right.
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): steps = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5] for five days. Answer many questions like "total steps from day l to day r".
Build prefix with a 0 in front: [0, 3, 4, 8, 9, 14]. prefix[i] is the total of the first i days.
Days 1 to 3: prefix[4] − prefix[1] = 9 − 3 = 6, and indeed 1 + 4 + 1 = 6. Days 0 to 4: prefix[5] − prefix[0] = 14.
Both sides of i, a second practice problem: in profits [2, 3, −1, 8, 4], find the index where the sum on its left equals the sum on its right.
total = 16. Carry left, the sum before i; then right = total − left − nums[i]. i = 0: 0 vs 14. i = 1: 2 vs 11. i = 2: 5 vs 12. i = 3: 4 vs 4, so the answer is 3.
Add nums[i] to left after each check. One pass after the total: O(n) time and O(1) memory.

blocks.title: Regularisation: L1, L2 and early stopping
blocks.builds_on: Day 14 · overfitting and the training–validation gap, and Day 7 · gradient descent on a loss
points: Regularisation fights overfitting (Day 14) by making complexity cost something. Training minimises loss + λ × a penalty on the weights.
L2 (ridge) adds λ × the sum of the squared weights. Big weights cost a lot, so every weight shrinks toward 0, but almost never reaches exactly 0.
L1 (lasso) adds λ × the sum of the absolute weights. It pushes many weights to exactly 0, so it also picks the features for you.
λ (lambda, the regularisation rate) sets the strength. 0 means no penalty; too large squeezes every weight toward 0 and the model underfits. Choose λ on the validation set, never on test (Day 10).
In gradient descent (Day 7), L2 adds 2λw to each weight's slope, so every step also shrinks w a little. That is why L2 is also called weight decay.
Scale the features first (Day 10's StandardScaler), so the penalty treats every weight fairly. The bias b is usually not penalised.

Early stopping: track the validation loss while training, and stop when it hasn't improved for a few rounds (the patience), keeping the best weights. Training loss keeps falling; validation loss turns back up once the model starts memorising.
blocks.say: Regularisation adds a weight penalty to the loss: L2 shrinks every weight, L1 sets some to zero and so picks features, and early stopping halts training when validation loss stops improving; I tune the strength on the validation set.
example: Day 14's degree-12 fit (seed 5), with x scaled to −1…1: training MSE 0.03, validation 0.95. Its biggest weight is 373, which lets the curve swing wildly between the training points.
Add L2 (scikit-learn's Ridge; its alpha is λ). At λ = 0.01: training 0.04, validation 0.13, and the biggest weight is 2.5. Same 12 features, a calmer curve.
Too strong, at λ = 100: training 0.43, validation 0.67. Every weight is squeezed near 0, so now it underfits.
L1 (Lasso) at λ = 0.001: validation 0.13, and 7 of the 12 weights are exactly 0. It chose its own features.
Early stopping in a training loop: validation loss by epoch is 0.50, 0.31, 0.22, 0.20, 0.21, 0.23, 0.26. With patience 3, training stops after epoch 7 and keeps the epoch-4 weights.

title: Sets for groups, runs of values · Strategy pattern

blocks.title: Arrays & Hashing: a set per group, and finding runs by sorting or hashing
blocks.builds_on: Day 8 · set vs sort-first for "seen before?", Day 9 · check before you store, and Day 11 · choosing a grouping key
points: Two patterns today, both built from tools you already use: sets kept per group, and runs of consecutive values.
"No repeats within each group": keep a dict of sets, seen[group_key]. For each item, work out every group it belongs to and check that group's set before adding to it (Day 9).
The skill is the key, as on Day 11: a row number, a column number, or a tuple you compute from the position. One item can belong to several groups at once, so check them all.
When the input has a fixed small size, such as a 9 × 9 grid, the work is O(1) in Big-O terms. Still say it as O(rows × cols) and explain why.
Runs of consecutive values (5, 6, 7) hide in unsorted data. Sorting puts them side by side, so one walk finds every run: O(n log n).

A set answers "is x + 1 here?" in O(1), which can beat sorting. The catch: walking a run from every one of its members repeats work, O(n²) on one long run. Ask which numbers are worth starting a walk from.
Decide how repeats count: 3, 3, 4 is a run of length 2. Make sure your walk skips duplicates.
Edge cases: an empty list, all values equal, negative numbers, and one long run.
blocks.say: For "no repeats per group" I keep a dict of sets keyed by the group; for runs of consecutive values I either sort and walk neighbours in O(n log n), or use a set for O(1) lookups and make sure no run is walked twice.
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): booked seats [12, 4, 5, 13, 1, 6, 14, 3]. List the blocks of neighbouring seats.
Walk with start = 1. The next seat, 3, isn't 1 + 1, so close the block 1–1 and start a new one at 3. Seats 4, 5 and 6 each follow on.
12 isn't 6 + 1: close 3–6. Seats 13 and 14 follow on, and the list ends: close 12–14.
Blocks: 1, 3–6 and 12–14. One sort and one walk: O(n log n) time. A set version can reach O(n); that is today's second problem to work out.

blocks.title: Strategy pattern: swap behaviour without if-else chains
blocks.builds_on: Day 9 · open/closed (one class per case behind an abstract method, plus a dict), and Day 14 · passing dependencies in
points: Strategy: put each interchangeable way of doing one job (an algorithm) behind one small interface. The object that needs the job (the context) holds one strategy and calls it.
Three parts: a Strategy interface (an ABC with one method), concrete strategies (one class per way), and the context, which receives a strategy and passes the work to it.
It is Day 9's open/closed fix with a name. A new way is a new class, and the context never changes.
The strategy is passed in (Day 14's dependency inversion), so it can be swapped while the program runs: through the constructor, a setter, or an argument per call.
In Python, functions are objects, so a strategy can be a plain function, or a dict from name to function. Use classes when a strategy needs its own settings or state.
Choosing which strategy (from config, user input or a request) happens in one place, often a dict lookup, never in an if/elif inside the context.
Don't reach for it for two cases that will never grow; a plain if is clearer. Use it when the cases grow, or must be swapped and tested separately.
blocks.say: Strategy puts each interchangeable algorithm behind one small interface and passes it into the object that uses it, so adding or swapping a behaviour is a new class or function, never a new elif.
example: A ride app prices trips with if mode == "normal": km × 12, elif "surge": km × 12 × 1.5, elif "pool": km × 8. Every new mode edits this tested method.
Strategy interface: class FareStrategy(ABC) with an abstract fare(km). NormalFare, SurgeFare(multiplier) and PoolFare implement it.
Context: Trip(km, pricing) stores a FareStrategy, and trip.price() returns self.pricing.fare(self.km). Trip never looks at the mode.
Swap while running: at 6 pm the app hands new trips SurgeFare(1.5), and at 8 pm NormalFare(). A late-night mode is one new class.
Function version: PRICING = {"normal": lambda km: km * 12, "pool": lambda km: km * 8}, and Trip takes any callable. Fine while a strategy needs no settings of its own.

title: One pass with a few variables · Precision, recall, F1

blocks.title: Arrays & Hashing: one pass with a few running variables, and majority voting
blocks.builds_on: Day 10 · Majority Element and its O(1)-memory follow-up, and Day 15 · carrying a running value through one pass
points: Many array questions need only a few numbers carried through one pass (a best so far, a current run, a candidate), not a dict of everything. That turns O(n) memory into O(1).
To design one, ask: what is the least I must remember about the items I've passed, to deal with the next one?
Before coding a "best total" question, sketch the numbers on paper first.
If you take the best local choice at each step (a greedy idea), test it: try to beat it on a small case by hand. If you can't, say why it is safe.
Majority voting (Boyer–Moore): keep a candidate and a count. A matching item adds 1, a different one takes 1 away, and when the count is 0 the next item becomes the candidate. O(n) time, O(1) memory.
Why it works: a value that fills more than half the list can't be cancelled out by all the others together, so it is the candidate left at the end.
Voting only names a candidate. If the question doesn't promise a majority exists, count the candidate in a second pass.
blocks.say: When O(1) memory is asked, I work out the least I must remember about the items I've passed and carry just that through one pass; for a majority, that is a candidate and a count that cancels against other values.
example: Day 10's follow-up, taught properly: votes [B, A, A, C, A, B, A]. Find the value that fills more than half, with O(1) memory.
B: the count is 0, so B becomes the candidate, count 1. A: different, count 0. A: count 0, so A becomes the candidate, count 1. C: count 0.
A: count 0, so candidate A, count 1. B: count 0. A: candidate A, count 1.
End: candidate A. A second pass counts A 4 times out of 7, more than half, so A is the answer.
Without the promise: in [A, B, C], voting ends on C, but C appears only once. The second pass catches that.

blocks.title: Classification metrics: precision, recall, F1
blocks.builds_on: Day 8 · the threshold that turns a probability into yes or no, and Day 10 · scoring on the validation set, where only 5% of loans defaulted
points: A confusion matrix counts four outcomes: true positives (said yes, was yes), false positives (said yes, was no), false negatives (said no, was yes) and true negatives (said no, was no).
Accuracy = correct ÷ all. With rare positives it misleads: if 1% of payments are fraud, a model that always says "not fraud" is 99% accurate and catches nothing.
Precision = TP ÷ (TP + FP): of the items you flagged, how many were right. Low precision means many false alarms.
Recall = TP ÷ (TP + FN): of the real positives, how many you caught. Low recall means many misses.
The threshold (Day 8) trades them. Raise it and you flag fewer, so precision usually rises and recall falls; lower it for the reverse.
Pick by what each mistake costs. A spam filter that bins a real email hurts, so favour precision. Cancer screening or fraud alerts: a miss hurts more, so favour recall.
F1 = 2 × P × R ÷ (P + R), the harmonic mean. It is high only when both are: P = 1.0 and R = 0.1 give F1 ≈ 0.18, not 0.55.
Measure on the validation set (Day 10), for the class you care about, and say which mistake matters more.
blocks.say: Precision is how many of my flags were right and recall is how many real positives I caught; I trade them with the threshold by the cost of a false alarm versus a miss, and use F1 when I need one number that reflects both.
example: A fraud model checks 1,000 payments, of which 40 are fraud. It flags 50, and 30 of those are fraud.
Accuracy = (30 + 940) / 1,000 = 97%. A model that always says "no" scores 96% and catches nothing, so accuracy says little here.
Lower the threshold: it now flags 120 and catches 38. Precision = 38 / 120 ≈ 0.32, recall = 38 / 40 = 0.95. Fewer misses, far more false alarms.
