blocks.title: Arrays & Hashing: prefix sums plus a dict, for subarrays with negative numbers
blocks.builds_on: Day 15 · prefix sums, Day 9 · complement lookup in a dict, and Day 3 · why a shrinking window needs numbers ≥ 0
points: A subarray is a run of neighbouring items. From Day 15, its sum is prefix[r + 1] − prefix[l]: the difference of two prefix sums.
Day 3's sliding window shrinks when the sum is too big. With negative numbers, shrinking can make the sum bigger, so the window rule breaks. Prefix sums don't care about signs.
Brute force: try every (l, r) pair. O(n²) with prefix sums, O(n³) without.

Day 9's trick, moved to prefixes: walk once, keep a running prefix sum, and ask a dict about the prefixes you've already passed, the way Two Sum asked about earlier numbers. Each item is one O(1) question.
What to store for each prefix depends on what the question asks; decide it before coding. The example below stores the first index.
Seed the dict with the empty prefix (sum 0, before index 0), so a subarray that starts at index 0 is found too.
Order matters, as in Two Sum: ask about earlier prefixes before you store the current one.
blocks.say: A subarray's sum is the difference of two prefix sums, so I walk once with a running prefix and ask a dict about earlier prefixes: O(n), and unlike a sliding window it works with negative numbers.
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): daily profits [3, 4, −7, 1, 2, −3]. Find the longest run of days whose total is exactly 0.
Two equal prefix sums mean the days between them add up to 0. Keep first[prefix] = the first index where that prefix appeared, seeded with first[0] = −1 for the empty prefix.
i = 0: s = 3, new, so first[3] = 0. i = 1: s = 7, first[7] = 1. i = 2: s = 0, seen at −1, so days 0–2 (3 + 4 − 7) make a run of length 3.
i = 3: s = 1, store it. i = 4: s = 3, seen at 0, so days 1–4, length 4. i = 5: s = 0, seen at −1, so days 0–5, length 6.
Keep only the first index of each prefix, since the earliest start gives the longest run. One pass: O(n) time and O(n) memory, and the negatives caused no trouble.

blocks.title: API design: REST, pagination, idempotency
blocks.builds_on: Day 4 · HTTP methods and status codes, and Day 6 · stateless servers, where any server may answer any request
points: REST models an API as resources (nouns) at URLs, acted on with HTTP methods: GET /orders/42 reads, POST /orders creates, PUT /orders/42 replaces it whole, PATCH /orders/42 changes some fields, DELETE /orders/42 removes.

Use plural nouns and nest for ownership (GET /users/7/orders). Use status codes that mean what they say: 201 created, 400 bad input, 401 not logged in, 403 not allowed, 404 missing, 409 conflict, 429 too many requests.
Put a version in the path (/v1/…) so old app versions keep working when a response changes.

Paginate every list that can grow. Offset paging (?limit=20&offset=40) is simple, but the database still walks past the skipped rows, and an insert meanwhile shifts every page, so items repeat or go missing.

Cursor paging: each response carries a next_cursor, say the last id seen, and the next request asks for items after it (WHERE id < cursor ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 20). It stays stable under inserts and fast at any depth; the cost is no jumping to page 7.
Idempotent means doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent by definition. POST is not, so a retried POST /payments could charge twice.

The fix: the client sends an Idempotency-Key header, a random id for each user action. The server saves key → result, and a repeat with the same key gets the saved result instead of a second charge. Keys expire after, say, 24 hours.
Retries are normal: a phone loses signal, a client times out and tries again, a proxy retries a failed request. Anything that creates things or moves money must be safe to retry.
blocks.say: I model resources as nouns with HTTP verbs and honest status codes, page lists with a cursor so they stay stable and fast, and make create-or-pay endpoints safe to retry with an idempotency key the server remembers.
example: Day 11's food-delivery app: POST /v1/orders places an order, GET /v1/orders/{id} reads one, and GET /v1/users/{id}/orders lists a user's orders.
Placing an order returns 201 Created with the order. Unknown items give 400; a restaurant that has just closed gives 409.
The list: GET /v1/users/7/orders?limit=20 returns 20 orders, newest first, plus next_cursor = the id of the 20th. The app then asks ?limit=20&cursor=<that id>.
A new order arrives while he scrolls. With offsets, every page shifts by one and an order shows twice; the cursor still starts right after the last order he saw.
He taps Pay, the network drops, and the app retries. Both requests carry Idempotency-Key: 9f1c…, so the server finds the key on the second one and returns the first result instead of charging again.

selftest.q: What does idempotent mean, and which HTTP methods are idempotent by definition?
selftest.a: Doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. GET, PUT and DELETE are; POST is not.

selftest.q: Why does offset pagination show repeats when new items arrive, and how does a cursor avoid it?
selftest.a: A new item at the top shifts every later item down one place, so the next offset page starts one item too early. A cursor asks for items after the last one seen, so inserts above it don't move the start.

selftest.q: Why does a sliding window fail for subarray sums when numbers can be negative, and what works instead?
selftest.a: Shrinking the window can make the sum bigger when a negative number leaves, so there is no safe rule for when to shrink. Prefix sums plus a dict of earlier prefixes work for any signs, in O(n).

selftest.q: In [2, −2, 3, 1, −4], is there a subarray with sum 0? Use prefix sums.
selftest.a: prefix = [0, 2, 0, 3, 4, 0]. The value 0 repeats, so yes: [2, −2] (prefixes 0 and 2), [3, 1, −4], and the whole list (prefixes 0 and 5), which is the longest.

selftest.q: A payments app's "Send money" request times out, the app retries, and the user is charged twice. Design the fix.
selftest.a: The app makes one Idempotency-Key per tap and sends it with every retry. The server stores key → result (scoped to the user) before replying; a repeat with that key returns the stored result without charging. Keys expire after about 24 hours.

points: Fridays start with revision. Re-solve what is in the Revise row from a blank file, then rate each one. Keep it to about 10 minutes; anything left shows again tomorrow.
Then a new topic, Two Pointers, starting with its plainest form: one index at each end, both moving inward until they meet.
Each step does a little work at the two ends and moves at least one pointer, so the loop ends after at most n steps: O(n) time and O(1) extra memory.
Loop while left < right. When they meet (odd length) or cross (even length), every pair has been handled; the middle item never needs to move.
Swapping is one line in Python: a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i]. "In place" (Day 12) means changing the given list and returning nothing.
Python strings can't be changed, so in-place work on text happens on a list of characters.
blocks.say: With one pointer at each end moving inward, I touch each item at most once and keep only two indexes: O(n) time, O(1) extra memory.
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): put the even numbers before the odd ones, in place, in [3, 8, 5, 2, 7, 6].
left = 0, right = 5. left stops on an odd number and right stops on an even one: 3 and 6. Swap: [6, 8, 5, 2, 7, 3]. Move both inward.
left passes 8 (even) and stops on 5 at index 2. right passes 7 (odd) and stops on 2 at index 3. Swap: [6, 8, 2, 5, 7, 3].
Move both: left = 3, right = 2. They have crossed, so stop. Evens 6, 8, 2 come first.
Each index was passed once: O(n) time, and only two indexes of extra memory.

blocks.title: Memory: virtual memory, paging and the TLB
blocks.builds_on: Day 5 · each process has its own memory, and a process switch costs more because the memory view changes
points: Every process sees its own virtual address space, as if it had the memory to itself. The CPU's memory unit (MMU) and the OS translate each virtual address into a physical one.
Why: isolation (one process can't read another's memory), and every program can be written as if it starts at address 0 with plenty of room.
Paging cuts memory into fixed-size pages, usually 4 KB. Each virtual page maps to a physical frame of the same size, so any free frame will do.
A virtual address splits into a page number and an offset. The page table, one per process, maps page number → frame number; the offset stays the same.

The page table lives in memory, so every access would need an extra memory read. The TLB is a small, fast cache of recent translations inside the CPU. Most lookups hit it, because programs keep touching the same pages (locality).

A page fault: the page isn't in memory (never loaded, or moved out to disk). The OS loads it and the instruction runs again. Disk is thousands of times slower than memory, so a machine that faults constantly (thrashing) crawls.

Switching to another process changes the address space, so the TLB's entries no longer apply: they are flushed or tagged by process. That is part of why Day 5's process switch costs more than a thread switch.
blocks.say: Each process gets its own virtual address space; a page table maps its pages to physical frames, the TLB caches recent translations so most lookups are fast, and a page fault loads a missing page from disk.
example: The reading's tiny machine: 16-byte pages, and a page table that maps virtual page 0 → frame 3, 1 → 7, 2 → 5 and 3 → 2.
Virtual address 21: page = 21 // 16 = 1, offset = 21 % 16 = 5.
Page 1 is in frame 7, so the physical address is 7 × 16 + 5 = 117.
The TLB now holds 1 → 7. The next access, address 26 (page 1, offset 10), hits the TLB: 7 × 16 + 10 = 122, with no page-table read.
If page 2 had been moved out to disk, address 40 (page 2, offset 8) would cause a page fault: the OS loads the page into a free frame, updates the table, and the access runs again.

selftest.q: What does a page table map, and what does the TLB cache?
selftest.a: The page table maps a process's virtual page numbers to physical frame numbers. The TLB is a small cache in the CPU of recent page → frame translations, so most lookups skip reading the page table.

selftest.q: What is a page fault, and why is thrashing so slow?
selftest.a: An access to a page that isn't in memory; the OS loads it (often from disk) and retries the instruction. Thrashing means faulting constantly, and every fault waits on disk, which is thousands of times slower than memory.

blocks.title: Two Pointers: compare from both ends, skipping what doesn't count
blocks.builds_on: Day 19 · pointers from both ends, moving inward
points: Yesterday the two ends swapped. Today they compare: check a[left] against a[right], then move both inward. One mismatch answers the question early.
Real input has noise: spaces, punctuation, capital letters. You can skip it as you walk instead of building a cleaned copy first.
Skip with an inner while loop that also checks left < right, so it can't run off the end when everything is noise.
str.isalnum() is True for letters and digits, and comparing .lower() versions makes 'A' match 'a'.
Say both ways: a cleaned copy compared with its reverse is O(n) time and O(n) memory; the pointer version is O(n) time and O(1) memory.
Edge cases: an empty string, a string of only punctuation, and a single character.
blocks.say: I compare from both ends inward and skip what doesn't count with bounded inner loops, so the check is O(n) time with O(1) extra memory instead of building a cleaned copy.
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): does [1, 0, 2, 0, 0, 2, 1] read the same both ways if you ignore the zeros?
left = 0, right = 6: 1 and 1 match. Move both inward: left = 1, right = 5.
a[1] is 0, so left skips to 2. a[2] = 2 and a[5] = 2 match. Move both: left = 3, right = 4.
a[3] is 0, so left moves to 4 and stops there, because its skip loop also checks left < right. The pointers have met, so nothing is left to compare: True.
Each index was passed once by one pointer: O(n) time and O(1) memory, with no cleaned copy.

blocks.builds_on: Day 8 · Contains Duplicate with a set, Day 10 · Design HashSet, where a key picks its slot, and Day 12 · Sort Colors, rearranged in place
points: You solved Contains Duplicate (Day 8), Design HashSet (Day 10) and Sort Colors (Day 12). This hard combines them: a set's "is it here?", a key that picks its own slot, and rearranging the list in place.
Step 1, say the plain answers: try 1, 2, 3, … and scan the list each time, O(n²); or sort and walk, O(n log n); or put everything in a set and test 1, 2, 3, …, O(n) time but O(n) memory.
Step 2, the key fact: n numbers can cover at most the values 1 to n, so the answer is somewhere from 1 to n + 1. Values ≤ 0 or > n can't change the answer, so they need no slot.
Step 3: you only need a yes/no for each value from 1 to n, and the list has exactly n slots. Which slot could stand for value v?
Step 4: how can you mark a slot without losing the value stored there? The example shows one way. Check whether it survives today's values ≤ 0 or > n, and trace it on paper before coding.
Step 5: when marking is done, how do you read the answer off, and what is it if every slot is marked?

blocks.say: When the answer must lie in 1 to n + 1, the list itself can be the hash set: value v marks index v − 1, by flipping a sign or swapping it into place, for O(n) time and O(1) extra memory.
example: Practice problem (not NeetCode 250): [4, 3, 2, 7, 8, 2, 3, 1] holds n = 8 values from 1 to 8, some repeated. Which of 1 to 8 are missing? Use O(1) extra memory.
Mark by sign: for each value, take v = abs(value), because it may already have been flipped, and make the number at index v − 1 negative.
4 flips index 3, 3 flips index 2, 2 flips index 1, 7 flips index 6 and 8 flips index 7. The second 2 and 3 find their slots already negative. 1 flips index 0.
The list is now [−4, −3, −2, −7, 8, 2, −3, −1]. Indexes 4 and 5 are still positive, so 5 and 6 never appeared.
Two passes: O(n) time and no extra set. Today's hard adds values ≤ 0 or > n, which have no slot. Decide what to do with them before you mark anything.

blocks.title: Choosing a database: ACID, indexes, SQL vs NoSQL
blocks.builds_on: Day 6 · the single database as the next bottleneck, Day 11 · read and write estimates, and Day 13 · a cache in front of the database
points: A relational (SQL) database stores rows in tables with a fixed schema, links tables by keys and joins them in queries. PostgreSQL and MySQL are the usual picks.

A transaction groups writes so they act as one. ACID: Atomic (all or nothing), Consistent (rules such as "balance ≥ 0" always hold), Isolated (transactions running at once don't see each other's half-done work), Durable (once committed, it survives a crash).
An index is a sorted structure, usually a B-tree, from a column's values to the rows. A lookup takes O(log n) steps instead of scanning every row.
Indexes aren't free: every insert or update must also update each index, and they take disk space. Index the columns your hot queries filter and sort by, not every column.
A composite index on (user_id, created_at) serves "this user's orders, newest first" and queries on user_id alone, but not queries on created_at alone: it is sorted by its first column first.

NoSQL families: key-value (Redis, DynamoDB) for lookups by key; document (MongoDB) for nested records; wide-column (Cassandra) for huge write volumes read by a known key; graph (Neo4j) for relationships.
Most NoSQL stores scale out more easily but give up some of: joins, flexible queries, multi-row transactions. You shape the data around the queries you know you'll run.

To choose, start from the data's shape, the access patterns, the consistency it needs and the scale (Day 11). Default to PostgreSQL unless a clear need, such as a huge write volume or key-only access, points elsewhere, and say why.
blocks.say: I default to a relational database for transactions and flexible queries, add indexes for the hot queries knowing they slow writes, and pick a NoSQL store only when the access pattern or write volume clearly calls for it.
example: Day 11's food-delivery app: users, restaurants, orders and payments, with about 23 order writes and 580 history reads a second on average.

Recording the payment and marking the order paid must happen together, so a crash between them can't leave the two disagreeing. That needs an ACID transaction: PostgreSQL. (The card charge itself is a call to the payment gateway, made safe to retry with Day 18's idempotency key.)
Hot query: a user's orders, newest first. An index on orders(user_id, created_at) turns a scan of millions of rows into a few B-tree steps.
Menus are nested (categories → items → options) and read far more than written. A document store would fit, but PostgreSQL tables with Day 13's cache in front fit too, so keep one database.
Delivery partners send a GPS ping every few seconds, millions of writes an hour, read only by partner and time. That pattern suits a wide-column store such as Cassandra.
Verdict: PostgreSQL for orders and payments, Redis as the cache, and a separate store only for the GPS stream, each with a one-line reason.

selftest.q: What do the four letters of ACID stand for, in one line each?
selftest.a: Atomic: all of a transaction's writes happen or none do. Consistent: the database's rules always hold. Isolated: transactions running at once don't see each other's half-done work. Durable: once committed, it survives a crash.

selftest.q: What does an index make faster, and what does it make slower?

selftest.q: With an index on (user_id, created_at), which of these use it: WHERE user_id = 7; WHERE created_at > X; WHERE user_id = 7 ORDER BY created_at?

selftest.q: Why must the first missing positive of a list of n numbers lie between 1 and n + 1?
selftest.a: n numbers can cover at most n different values. If they are exactly 1 to n, the answer is n + 1; otherwise some value from 1 to n is missing, and the smallest one is the answer.

selftest.q: A ride app stores trips with fares and payments, plus a stream of driver GPS pings every few seconds. Which database for each, and why?

blocks.builds_on: Day 20 · comparing from both ends, and Day 1 · slicing copies what it takes
points: Some problems allow one fix: one deletion, one edit, one swap. The pointers walk as usual until the first mismatch, and only there do you spend the fix.
Check every way of spending it; if any works, the answer is yes.
The choice happens once and each check is O(n), so the total stays O(n), not O(2^n). Say that out loud: it is what interviewers ask next.
Compare by index rather than slicing new strings for each check (Day 1: a slice copies what it takes).
Edge cases: a mismatch at the very first or last pair, input that already passes with no fix, and lengths 1 and 2.
blocks.say: With one fix allowed, I walk the pointers to the first mismatch and spend the fix only there; one branching point keeps it O(n).
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): are "pale" and "ple" at most one edit apart (insert, delete or replace one character)?
Walk i on "pale" and j on "ple": p matches p. Then 'a' ≠ 'l' at i = 1, j = 1. Spend the one edit here.
The first string is longer, so the only fix is deleting from it: skip i, then check "le" (from i = 2) against "le" (from j = 1). They match: True.
"pale" vs "bake": 'p' ≠ 'b' with equal lengths, so the fix is a replace. Check "ale" against "ake": 'l' ≠ 'k' is a second mismatch, so False.
One branching point and one linear check: O(n) time, and O(1) memory if you compare by index.

blocks.title: Machine-coding playbook (entities, services, a driver) + build tic-tac-toe
blocks.builds_on: Day 2 · classes and dataclasses, Day 9 · one job per class, and Day 16 · Strategy, which is how a bot player plugs in
points: A machine-coding round gives 60 to 90 minutes to build a small system that runs. It is scored on working code, clean classes and how easily it extends, not on clever algorithms.
First 10 minutes, requirements: ask what is in and out of scope (board size? two humans or a bot? undo?), write the answers as a short list, and agree it before you code.
Entities are the nouns, with their data (Board, Player, Move). Services are the verbs that hold the rules (Game decides turns, checks moves and finds the winner).
A driver, main(), wires them together and does all input and output. Keep print and input out of the classes, so the rules can be tested without a keyboard.

Use an enum for a fixed set of values: `from enum import Enum`, then `class Status(Enum):` with one line per value (`IN_PROGRESS = 1`, `DRAW = 2`, …), used as `Status.DRAW`. Raise a clear exception for an illegal action such as a move on a taken cell.
Build in thin slices that each run: the board, then moves, then the win check, then the game loop. Run it after every slice.
Keep the last 10 to 15 minutes to play a scripted game, show the edge cases (a taken cell, a draw) and say how you would extend it.

Common extensions: an n × n board, k in a row, a bot player (Day 16: HumanPlayer and RandomBot behind one choose_move), and a faster win check that keeps a count per row, column and diagonal, so each move is checked in O(1).
blocks.say: In machine coding I agree the requirements first, put the nouns in entities and the rules in a service, keep all input and output in a thin driver, build in slices that run, and leave time to demo and discuss extensions.
example: A smaller system through the same playbook: best-of-three rock-paper-scissors. Requirements: two players, the first to win two rounds wins the match, and a tied round is replayed.
Entities: Move, an Enum of ROCK, PAPER and SCISSORS; Player(name, chooser). Service: Match, with play_round(move_a, move_b) and a status of IN_PROGRESS or WON.
The rule lives in one place: BEATS = {ROCK: SCISSORS, PAPER: ROCK, SCISSORS: PAPER}, and a beats b when BEATS[a] is b.
Driver: main() asks each player's chooser for a move, calls match.play_round, prints the result and stops once the status is WON. Match never calls print or input.
Test with a script: (ROCK, SCISSORS), (PAPER, PAPER), (PAPER, ROCK) gives player A the match 2–0, with the tie replayed. A RandomChooser bot is just another chooser: Day 16's Strategy.

tasks.text: 10 minutes, before any code: write tic-tac-toe's requirements as a list (3 × 3, players X and O take turns, three in a row, column or diagonal wins, a full board is a draw, illegal moves are rejected), then the entities and the service with their method names.

About 50 minutes: build it in Python in slices. Board with place(row, col, symbol) that raises on a taken or off-board cell; Player; Game with make_move(row, col), the current player and a status (IN_PROGRESS, X_WON, O_WON, DRAW); and a main() driver that reads moves typed as "row col". Run it after each slice.

About 15 minutes: write tests that play a scripted game to an X win and another to a draw, and assert the status. Then add a RandomBot with the same choose_move as the human player, and play human vs bot.

blocks.title: ROC curves, AUC and picking a threshold
blocks.builds_on: Day 17 · the confusion matrix, precision and recall, and Day 8 · the threshold
points: Every threshold gives a different confusion matrix. A ROC curve shows them all at once: one point per threshold.
Its axes: the true positive rate (TPR, which is recall: TP ÷ (TP + FN)) going up, and the false positive rate (FPR = FP ÷ (FP + TN), the share of negatives wrongly flagged) going across.
A threshold above every score flags nothing: point (0, 0). Flagging everything gives (1, 1). A good model bows toward the top-left corner (0, 1); the diagonal is random guessing.
AUC is the area under the curve: 1.0 is perfect and 0.5 is a coin flip. It also means the chance that a random positive gets a higher score than a random negative.
AUC compares models without choosing a threshold, and depends only on the order of the scores. It doesn't tell you which threshold to ship.
With very rare positives, FPR stays tiny even with many false alarms, because the negatives are so many, so the ROC curve looks great. A precision–recall curve shows the false alarms better there.
To pick the threshold, use the validation set (Day 10). Minimise the cost, FP × cost of a false alarm + FN × cost of a miss, or meet a target such as "recall at least 0.95" with the best precision.
blocks.say: A ROC curve plots recall against the false-positive rate across all thresholds, AUC is the chance a positive outranks a negative, and I pick the threshold to ship on validation data by the cost of false alarms versus misses.
example: Six validation emails, scored and labelled: 0.9 spam, 0.8 spam, 0.7 not, 0.6 spam, 0.4 not, 0.2 not. That is 3 spam and 3 not.
Flag scores ≥ the threshold. At 0.8: FPR 0, TPR 2/3. At 0.7: FPR 1/3, TPR 2/3. At 0.6: FPR 1/3, TPR 1. At 0.2: everything is flagged, FPR 1, TPR 1.
Joining the points (FPR, TPR) = (0, 0), (0, 1/3), (0, 2/3), (1/3, 2/3), (1/3, 1), (2/3, 1) and (1, 1) draws the ROC curve.
AUC by pairs: of the 3 × 3 = 9 (spam, not) pairs, the spam scores higher in 8; only 0.6 vs 0.7 is the wrong way round. AUC = 8/9 ≈ 0.89.
Costs: binning a real email (FP) costs 5, a missed spam (FN) costs 1. Threshold 0.8: 1 FN and 0 FP, cost 1. Threshold 0.6: 0 FN and 1 FP, cost 5. Ship 0.8.

selftest.q: What are the two axes of a ROC curve, and where do "flag nothing" and "flag everything" sit on it?

blocks.title: Two Pointers: one pointer per list, read and write pointers, and filling from the back
blocks.builds_on: Day 11 · the merge step of merge sort, Day 10 · in-place filtering with a write index, and Day 19 · Two Pointers from both ends
points: Days 19 to 21 moved two pointers toward each other. Today they move the same way: one pointer per input list, or a read pointer and a write pointer in the same list.
One pointer per list: at each step take from one list and move only that list's pointer. When one list runs out, copy the rest of the other. Day 11's merge step is exactly this.

Read and write in one list (Day 10): the read pointer visits every item and the write pointer marks where the next kept item goes. Write only moves when an item is kept, so it never passes read, and the kept items end up at the front in order.
Sorted input puts equal values side by side (Day 8), so "have I kept this value already?" needs no set. Work out what each item should be compared with.

Direction matters: if writing forwards could land on items you haven't read yet, try walking from the right instead, so the write pointer stays at or to the right of the read pointer. The worked example shows one case.
Python strings can't be changed (Day 19), so build text answers as a list of parts and `''.join` it once (Day 1).
Say the cost each time: O(n + m) time for two lists of n and m items, and O(1) extra memory when you work in place.
Edge cases: an empty list, lists of different lengths, and every item equal.
blocks.say: With same-direction pointers each item is read once: one pointer per list to merge, or a read and a write pointer to filter in place, walking from the right when writing forwards would overwrite unread items.
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): a character list holds "hi you" plus 2 spare slots at the end: ['h', 'i', ' ', 'y', 'o', 'u', _, _]. Replace the space with "%20" in place.
From the front, the space at index 2 would become '%', '2', '0' in slots 2 to 4, overwriting 'y' and 'o' before you have read them.
From the back: read = 5 (the last real character) and write = 7 (the last slot). Copy 'u', 'o' and 'y' into slots 7, 6 and 5, moving both pointers left each time.
read = 2 is the space: write '0', '2' and '%' into slots 4, 3 and 2. write is now 1, and read moves to 1.
Copy 'i' into slot 1 and 'h' into slot 0: "hi%20you". Each character was read once, O(n) time with no extra list, and write always stayed at or to the right of read.

blocks.title: Decision trees and random forests
blocks.builds_on: Day 8 · classification, Day 10 · the validation split, and Day 14 · overfitting and variance
points: A decision tree predicts by asking yes/no questions about the features, one at a time ("income < ₹30,000 a month?"). Each leaf gives the answer: the most common class for classification, or the average for regression.
Training is greedy: at each node, try every feature and threshold, and keep the split whose two groups are purest. Then do the same inside each group.

Gini impurity measures how mixed a group is: 1 − the sum of each class's share squared. A pure group scores 0; a 50/50 split of two classes scores 0.5. A split is scored by its groups' Gini, weighted by their sizes.
Trees need no feature scaling, handle yes/no and numeric features together, and are easy to explain: follow the path to the leaf.

Left to grow, a tree keeps splitting until every leaf is pure, so it memorises the training data: high variance (Day 14). Limit it with `max_depth` or `min_samples_leaf`, chosen on validation (Day 10).
A random forest trains many deep trees, each on a bootstrap sample (rows drawn at random with repeats) and with a random subset of features tried at each split. It predicts by majority vote.
The trees make different mistakes, and voting cancels many of them, so variance falls while bias stays about the same. Forests are a strong first model for table data.
Feature importance (how much each feature cut impurity across the trees) gives a quick first look at what the model uses, but it favours features with many distinct values.
blocks.say: A decision tree splits greedily on the feature that makes its groups purest, which overfits if it grows deep; a random forest averages many trees built on random rows and features, which cuts the variance.
example: Ten loan applicants: 4 defaulted and 6 repaid. Gini at the root = 1 − (0.4² + 0.6²) = 0.48.
Split A, "income < ₹30,000": the left group has 4 people (3 defaulted, 1 repaid), Gini 1 − (0.75² + 0.25²) = 0.375. The right group has 6 (1 defaulted, 5 repaid), Gini ≈ 0.278.
Weighted by size: 0.4 × 0.375 + 0.6 × 0.278 ≈ 0.317, down from 0.48.
Split B, "has a guarantor": 5 and 5, each with 2 defaults, so both groups are still 0.48. No gain, so the tree picks split A.
The left group is still mixed. A deeper tree splits it again; with `max_depth=1` it stops and predicts "default" there, because 3 of its 4 defaulted.

selftest.q: In a same-direction pass with a read and a write pointer, why does the write pointer never overwrite an item you still need?
selftest.a: Read moves every step and write moves only when an item is kept, so write is never ahead of read. Every slot write touches has already been read.

selftest.q: When do you walk a list from the right instead of the left?
selftest.a: When writing forwards would overwrite items you haven't read yet. Walking from the right keeps the write pointer at or to the right of the read pointer.

selftest.q: What is the Gini impurity of a group with 8 yes and 2 no?
Why does a random forest usually do better on new data than one deep tree?
selftest.a: One deep tree has high variance: it memorises its training rows. A forest votes across many trees built on different random rows and features, so their mistakes partly cancel. Variance falls while bias stays about the same.

selftest.q: Your unlimited tree scores 1.000 on training and 0.906 on validation. What is happening, and what are two fixes?
selftest.a: It is overfitting (high variance, Day 14). Limit the tree with max_depth or min_samples_leaf chosen on validation, or switch to a random forest.

title: Pair search on sorted data · Factory pattern

blocks.title: Two Pointers: on sorted data, each comparison drops one end
blocks.builds_on: Day 19 · pointers from both ends, Day 3 · opposite ends on sorted data, and Day 9 · Two Sum's dict of complements
points: Day 9 found a pair with a dict: O(n) time and O(n) memory, on data in any order. When the list is sorted, pointers from both ends can do it with O(1) extra memory.

Compare the pair at the two ends with what you need. On sorted data, if a[left] + a[right] is too small, a[left] with any partner left of right is smaller still, so a[left] is in no answer: move left on. Too big: drop a[right] the same way.
Each step rules out one item together with every pair it could still make, so at most n steps cover all n²/2 pairs: O(n) after sorting.
If the input isn't sorted, sorting first costs O(n log n) and loses the original positions. Ask whether the answer needs them.
Three items: fix one with an outer loop, then run the pair search on the items to its right. That is O(n²) instead of O(n³) for trying every triple.
If the answers must not repeat, work out where repeats come from in sorted data and skip them as you go, instead of collecting everything in a set at the end.
Read the output format: some problems count positions from 1, not 0.
Edge cases: no answer, every value equal, and negatives and zeros mixed in.
blocks.say: On sorted data I compare the two ends with what I need and drop the end that can't be in any answer, so one pass replaces checking every pair; for three items I fix one and pair-search the rest, O(n²).
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): how many triangles can you make from sticks [2, 2, 3, 4]? Three sticks make a triangle when the two shorter ones add up to more than the longest.

Sort, then fix the longest stick from the end. Longest = 4 (index 3), left = 0, right = 2: 2 + 3 = 5 > 4, so every stick from left up to right − 1 also works with the 3. Add right − left = 2 triangles, then move right down.
left = 0, right = 1: 2 + 2 = 4 is not more than 4, so move left up. The pointers meet: done with the 4.
Longest = 3 (index 2), left = 0, right = 1: 2 + 2 = 4 > 3, so add 1. Total 3: (2, 2, 3), and (2, 3, 4) twice, once with each 2.
Fixing one stick and pair-searching the rest is O(n²) instead of O(n³), because each comparison counted or dropped a whole run of pairs at once.

blocks.title: Factory pattern: one place that creates objects
blocks.builds_on: Day 16 · Strategy and choosing it in one place, Day 9 · open/closed, and Day 14 · depending on an interface
points: A factory is one place that decides which class to create, and creates it. Callers ask for "a payment for 'upi'" and get an object behind an interface; they never name the concrete class.

A simple factory in Python is a dict from name to class plus a function: `PAYMENTS = {"upi": UpiPayment, "card": CardPayment}`, and `make_payment(kind, **details)` looks the class up and calls it. Raise a clear ValueError for an unknown kind.
Why: the if/elif on a type lives in one place (Day 9's open/closed). A new kind is one new class and one dict entry, and the callers depend only on the interface (Day 14).

In Python a class is an object, so a dict of classes is often the whole factory. Don't build a factory class hierarchy for two kinds that will never grow. Day 9's DISCOUNTS dict held ready-made objects to reuse; a factory's dict holds classes, so each call builds a new object with its own details, such as a UPI id or a card token.
Factory Method, the book version: a base class's method calls an abstract `create_…()` method that each subclass overrides, so the subclass decides which object the base class's own code works with.
Abstract Factory, for recognition only: one object creates a family of parts that must match, such as a dark theme's button and its checkbox.
Strategy (Day 16) decides which behaviour an object uses; a factory creates the right object. They often meet: a factory reads the config and builds the strategy.
blocks.say: A factory keeps the decision of which class to create in one place, in Python usually a dict from name to class, so callers depend only on the interface and a new kind is one new class plus one entry.
example: Checkout creates payments with `if method == "upi": UpiPayment(vpa) elif method == "card": CardPayment(token) …`, and the refunds code has a copy of the same chain.

Simple factory: `PAYMENTS = {"upi": UpiPayment, "card": CardPayment}`, and `make_payment(method, **details)` does `cls = PAYMENTS.get(method)`, raises ValueError if cls is None, and returns `cls(**details)`.
Checkout now calls `make_payment(req.method, **req.details).pay(amount)` and knows only the Payment ABC (Day 7). Refunds call the same function.
Adding net banking is one NetBankingPayment class and one dict entry. Checkout and refunds don't change (Day 9).
With Strategy (Day 16): `make_fare(config["mode"])` returns `SurgeFare(1.5)` or `NormalFare()`, so Trip still just receives a FareStrategy.

selftest.q: On a sorted list, a[left] + a[right] is smaller than the target. Why can you move left on without missing an answer?
selftest.a: Every other partner for a[left] is at most a[right], so all of its sums are smaller still. a[left] is in no answer.

selftest.q: Fixing one item and pair-searching the rest: what does it cost, and why?
selftest.a: O(n²): n choices for the fixed item, and an O(n) two-pointer pass for each one. The O(n log n) sort first is smaller, so it doesn't change the total.

selftest.q: What is a simple factory in Python, and what goes wrong without one?
selftest.a: A function plus a dict from name to class that creates the right object. Without it, the same if/elif on a type is copied wherever objects are made, and every new kind means editing all of the copies.

selftest.q: Strategy and Factory: what is each one about?
selftest.a: Strategy: which behaviour an object uses, swapped behind one interface. Factory: creating the right object in one place. A factory often builds the strategy from config.

selftest.q: Sorted [1, 3, 4, 6, 9], target 13. Trace the two pointers.
selftest.a: 1 + 9 = 10 is too small, so left moves to 3. 3 + 9 = 12 is too small, so left moves to 4. 4 + 9 = 13: found, at indexes 2 and 4.

title: Fixing more items, moving round a circle · Gradient boosting

blocks.title: Two Pointers: more items by fixing more, and moving items round a circle
blocks.builds_on: Day 23 · fixing one item and pair-searching the rest, Day 19 · swapping in place from both ends, and Day 12 · what "in place" means
points: Yesterday three items became one loop plus a pair search. Four items add one more loop: fix two, then pair-search the rest. Each extra item multiplies the work by n, so four items is O(n³).
Skipping repeats now has to happen at every loop that picks a value, not only the innermost. Check each loop on an input like [2, 2, 2, 2, 2].
Python's integers never overflow, but in Java or C++ the sum of four large numbers can. Say so if asked.
Moving round a circle: an item at index i that moves k steps lands at (i + k) % n. If k ≥ n, only k % n matters, because n steps bring every item back to where it started.
Write the plain version first with a new list, and say its cost: O(n) time and O(n) memory. Then try the O(1)-memory follow-up.

For the follow-up, draw the list before and after on paper and look for a pattern in how its two parts moved. If 15 minutes pass with no plan, watch only the idea in the row's Video link, then close it and code it.
Edge cases: k = 0, k = n, k bigger than n, and a list of one item.
blocks.say: For k items I fix k − 2 of them with loops and pair-search the rest, skipping repeats at every level; for moving round a circle the new index is (i + k) % n, so only k % n steps matter.
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): six guests sit in seats 0 to 5 at a round table, and everyone moves 4 seats clockwise. Where does each guest end up?
The guest in seat 1 goes to (1 + 4) % 6 = 5. The guest in seat 3 goes to (3 + 4) % 6 = 1: past seat 5 the count wraps round to 0.
With k = 16 the answer is the same as with k = 4, because 16 % 6 = 4: twelve of the steps take everyone all the way round twice.
Plain version: `new = [None] * 6`, then `new[(i + k) % 6] = guests[i]` for each i. One pass: O(n) time, and O(n) memory for the new list.
Writing straight into the old list instead would overwrite a guest before they had moved. Doing it without the second list is today's follow-up.

blocks.title: Gradient boosting: trees that fix each other's mistakes
blocks.builds_on: Day 22 · decision trees and random forests, Day 7 · gradient descent, and Day 15 · early stopping
points: Boosting builds trees one after another, and each new tree fixes the errors left by all the trees before it. A random forest (Day 22) builds deep trees independently and votes; boosting adds small, shallow trees in sequence.

For regression: start every prediction at one number, the mean. The residual is truth minus prediction, the opposite sign of Day 3's error, so adding a tree's guess moves each prediction toward the truth. Fit a small tree to the residuals, add learning rate × its output to every prediction, and repeat.

Why "gradient": for squared error, the residuals point the way the loss falls fastest, so each tree is one step of gradient descent (Day 7). For other losses, such as log loss (Day 8), the trees fit that loss's gradient instead.
The learning rate (also called shrinkage), often 0.05 to 0.1, keeps each tree's step small. Smaller steps need more trees but usually do better on new data.
Every tree lowers the training loss, so with too many trees boosting overfits. Watch the validation loss and stop when it stops falling: Day 15's early stopping.

Main settings: the number of trees, the learning rate, the tree depth (often 2 to 8) and the share of rows each tree sees. XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost are the well-known libraries; scikit-learn has GradientBoostingClassifier and the faster HistGradientBoostingClassifier.

The interview contrast: a forest mainly lowers variance and is hard to overfit by adding trees; boosting mainly lowers bias, is often the most accurate model on table data, and needs its learning rate and stopping point tuned.
blocks.say: Gradient boosting adds small trees one at a time, each fitted to the current errors and scaled by a learning rate, which is gradient descent done with trees; I stop adding trees when the validation loss stops falling.
example: Three flats with rents of 10, 20 and 60 (thousand ₹), smallest flat first. Start every prediction at the mean, 30. Residuals: −20, −10 and +30. MSE ≈ 467.

Tree 1 makes one split, the first two flats against the third, and predicts each side's average residual: −15, −15, +30. With a learning rate of 0.5, the predictions become 22.5, 22.5 and 45. MSE ≈ 129.
New residuals: −12.5, −2.5 and +15. Tree 2's best split is the same one, predicting −7.5, −7.5 and +15. Adding half gives 18.75, 18.75 and 52.5. MSE ≈ 45.
Each tree fixes part of what is left, and the learning rate stops any one tree from over-correcting. Training error keeps falling toward 0; validation error does not.
In a classifier the trees fit the gradient of log loss instead, and the summed scores go through the sigmoid (Day 8) to become probabilities.

selftest.q: Random forest and gradient boosting: how are their trees built, and which kind of error does each mainly reduce?

blocks.title: Two Pointers: greedy moves from both ends, and why they are safe
blocks.builds_on: Day 23 · moving one end by a comparison, Day 17 · testing a greedy idea by hand, and Day 8 · sorting first
points: On Day 23 each comparison with a target said which end to move. Today there is no target: you want the biggest or the smallest score, and each move has to be argued.
The argument: show that the end you drop can't be part of a better answer than one you have already counted. If you can say that sentence, dropping it loses nothing.
Before coding a "best pair" question, write a pair's score as a formula. Then ask, for each end: if I move it inward, what can happen to each part of the score?

If the order of the input doesn't matter, sorting first puts the extremes at the two ends, where these pointers start. Some moves are forced: an end that can never be part of any answer as it stands must change, as in the example.
Test a greedy idea the Day 17 way: try to beat it by hand on a small case. If you can't, say why it is safe.
Say the brute force first, every pair in O(n²). Each greedy step drops at least one end, so the pass is O(n), plus O(n log n) if you sort.
Edge cases: two items, every item equal, and an item that can't be paired with anyone.
blocks.say: Each step drops one end, and I justify it by showing that end can't be part of a better answer than one I've already counted; that turns O(n²) pairs into one O(n) pass after sorting.
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): positive numbers [3, 2, 1, 4, 2]. One merge replaces two neighbours with their sum. Use as few merges as possible to make the list read the same both ways.

Pointers at the two ends: 3 and 2. The finished list must start and end with equal numbers. The right block, 2, is smaller than anything the left block can become, so it must grow: merging it with its neighbour is forced. [3, 2, 1, 6], 1 merge.
3 against 6: now the left end is smaller, so it is forced to merge: [5, 1, 6]. 5 against 6: still smaller, merge again: [6, 6]. 3 merges.

6 against 6: the ends already match, so both are settled. Keeping them as the outer pair costs no merge, and growing one would force the other side to grow by the same amount, which can't save a merge. Move both pointers in; they meet, so stop. Answer: 3 merges.

Why it is safe: every merge was forced, since the smaller end could never match the other side without growing, so any answer must make it too. Each step merges once or settles both ends: one O(n) pass, where brute force would try every way of cutting the list.

blocks.title: Unique IDs: UUID, Snowflake, base62 short codes
blocks.builds_on: Day 20 · primary keys and B-tree indexes, Day 6 · many servers behind a load balancer, and Day 11 · estimates
points: One database's auto-increment id works until many servers or databases create rows at once. Then a single counter becomes a bottleneck and a single point of failure.

UUID v4: 122 random bits, made anywhere with no coordination; a clash is practically impossible. The costs: 16 bytes (36 characters as text), and random order scatters inserts across a B-tree index (Day 20), which slows writes.
UUID v7 puts a millisecond timestamp first and random bits after, so new ids land at the end of the index. Same size, much kinder to the index.

Snowflake (Twitter): a 64-bit number made of 1 unused sign bit, 41 bits of milliseconds since a chosen start date, 10 bits of machine id and 12 bits of sequence. Each machine can make 4,096 ids per millisecond, and the ids sort by time and fit in a BIGINT.

Snowflake's catches: every machine needs its own id (from config or a coordinator), and a clock that jumps backwards could repeat ids, so the generator must wait or refuse. 41 bits of milliseconds last about 69 years.
Base62 writes a number with 0–9, a–z and A–Z: 62 symbols, all safe in a URL. Seven characters cover 62⁷ ≈ 3.5 trillion codes.

Short codes come from a counter turned into base62 (each server takes a block of numbers at a time, so it doesn't ask for every one), or from a hash of the long URL cut short, which can clash and needs a uniqueness check. Counter codes are guessable; add randomness if that matters.
To choose: no coordination and size doesn't matter, UUID (v7 for the index); compact, time-sorted and fast, Snowflake; short codes people see, base62 of a counter.
blocks.say: I pick ids by need: UUIDs when any machine must make them without coordination, Snowflake-style 64-bit ids when I want them compact and sorted by time, and base62 of a counter for short codes people see.
example: Base62 digits: 0–9 are 0 to 9, a–z are 10 to 35, and A–Z are 36 to 61.
Encode 11,157: 11,157 = 179 × 62 + 59, and 179 = 2 × 62 + 55, and 2 = 0 × 62 + 2. Reading the remainders last to first gives 2, 55, 59, which is "2TX".
Decode: (2 × 62 + 55) × 62 + 59 = 11,157. One more character multiplies the space by 62.
Snowflake: 1,000,000 ms after the start date, machine 5, sequence 3. `x << 22` means x × 2²², and `|` joins bit fields that don't overlap: `(1_000_000 << 22) | (5 << 12) | 3` = 4,194,304,020,483.
The sequence takes the low 12 bits and the machine the next 10, so the timestamp starts at bit 22. A later millisecond always gives a bigger id, which is why Snowflake ids sort by time.

blocks.builds_on: Day 19 · Friday revision, Day 3 · a fixed window with a running sum, and Day 2 · sets and count dicts
points: Fridays start with revision. Re-solve what is in the Revise row from a blank file, then rate each one. Keep it to about 10 minutes; anything left shows again tomorrow.
Then a new topic, Sliding Window, starting with its plainest form: a window of fixed size k that moves one step at a time.

Keep a summary of what is inside the window: a running sum (Day 3), a set, or a count dict. Each move adds the item that enters and removes the one that leaves: O(1) per move instead of rebuilding the window.
With a count dict, lower the leaving item's count and delete its key when it reaches 0, so `len(counts)` stays the number of different items in the window.
The first k − 1 steps are special because the window is still filling. Decide whether the question cares about windows shorter than k.
Each item enters once and leaves once: O(n) time, and O(k) memory for the summary.
blocks.say: A fixed-size window keeps a summary of its k items and updates it for the one item entering and the one leaving, so each step is O(1) and the whole pass is O(n).
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): sensor ids [5, 1, 5, 2, 2, 7]. How many different sensors report in each window of 3 readings?
First window [5, 1, 5]: counts {5: 2, 1: 1}, so 2 different.
Slide: 2 enters and the first 5 leaves. counts {5: 1, 1: 1, 2: 1}: 3 different.
2 enters and 1 leaves: 1's count reaches 0, so delete it. counts {5: 1, 2: 2}: 2. Then 7 enters and 5 leaves: {2: 2, 7: 1}: 2.
Answer [2, 3, 2, 2]. Each reading was added once and removed once: O(n).

blocks.title: Race conditions, critical sections and mutexes
blocks.builds_on: Day 5 · threads share their process's memory, and the GIL, and Day 12 · the scheduler can pause a thread when its time slice ends
points: A race condition: the result depends on how the threads' steps happen to interleave. Day 5 said shared memory needs locks; this is why.
`count += 1` is three steps: read count, add 1, write it back. If two threads both read 5 before either writes, both write 6, and one update is lost.
The GIL (Day 5) runs one thread at a time, but a switch can fall between the read and the write, so Python threads still race.
A critical section is the code that touches shared data and must run in one thread at a time.

A mutex (a lock) guards it: take the lock before, release it after, and any other thread that asks for it waits. In Python: `lock = threading.Lock()` and `with lock:`, which releases the lock even if an exception is raised.
Check-then-act is a race too: `if key not in cache: cache[key] = load(key)` lets two threads both see the key missing. The check and the act must sit under the same lock.
Keep critical sections short: everything inside runs one thread at a time, so a slow call inside a lock makes every thread queue.
Two threads that each hold one lock and wait for the other's are stuck for good: a deadlock. Taking locks in the same order everywhere avoids it; Day 40 covers it properly.
blocks.say: A race condition happens when threads interleave a read-modify-write on shared data; I put the whole read, check and write in one short critical section guarded by a mutex, in Python `with lock:`.
example: Two threads each run `count += 1` once, starting from count = 5. The line is three steps: read count, add 1, write it back.
Thread A reads 5. The scheduler pauses A (Day 12) and runs B, which also reads 5, adds 1 and writes 6.
A resumes with its old 5, adds 1 and writes 6. Two increments ran, but count went up by one: a lost update.
With a lock, A takes it, then reads, adds and writes. B's `with lock:` waits until A releases it, then B reads 6 and writes 7.
The lock turned the three steps into one critical section that only one thread can be inside at a time.

selftest.q: What is a race condition, in one sentence?
selftest.a: A bug where the result depends on how the threads' steps happen to interleave, such as two threads both reading a value before either writes it back.

selftest.q: What is a critical section, and how does a mutex protect it in Python?
selftest.a: The code that touches shared data and must run in one thread at a time. `lock = threading.Lock()`, then `with lock:` around that code: other threads wait until it is released, even if an exception is raised inside.

selftest.q: Why is `if key not in cache: cache[key] = load(key)` unsafe with threads, even though each line looks harmless?

selftest.q: In a fixed window with a count dict, why delete a key when its count reaches 0?

blocks.title: Sliding Window: a window whose left end jumps
blocks.builds_on: Day 26 · a window of fixed size, Day 3 · a window that shrinks while it breaks its rule, and Day 17 · the least you must remember
points: Day 26's window had a fixed size. Most windows don't: the right end moves every step, and the left end moves only when the rule says the window should start later.
Two ways to move the left end. Creep: drop one item at a time while the window breaks its rule (Day 3). Jump: move it straight to a new position in one step.
A jump is safe only when you can say why no window starting before the new position can ever win again. Say that sentence out loud before coding.
Often the window needs no list or dict at all, only where it starts and the best answer so far (Day 17: the least you must remember).
Update the best answer as the window changes, not only at the end.
Edge cases: one item, every item the same, and the best window right at the start.
blocks.say: In a variable window the right end moves every step and the left end moves only when the rule says so, creeping one step at a time or jumping straight to a better start, so the pass stays O(n).
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): readings [3, 5, 5, 2, 4, 6, 7, 1]. Find the longest run where each reading is at least the one before it.
start = 0. 5 ≥ 3 and 5 ≥ 5, so the window grows to [3, 5, 5]: length 3.
2 < 5 breaks the rule. Every window that starts before index 3 contains that drop, so jump: start = 3.
4, 6 and 7 each follow on: [2, 4, 6, 7], length 4, the best so far. Then 1 < 7, so jump again: start = 7.
Answer 4. One pass keeping only start and best: O(n) time and O(1) memory.

points: You solved Product of Array Except Self (Day 15) and Container With Most Water (Day 25). This hard combines them: a value at each index that depends on what lies on both sides of it, and two pointers moving in from the ends that must decide which side to move.

Step 1, one index at a time: draw some bars and pour water over a single index. Its water level is set by two walls. Which two, and why does one of them decide? Write the water at index i as a formula, and say the O(n²) brute force that rescans both sides for each i.

Step 3, O(1) memory: a pointer at each end, each with its own running value. At each step ask: on which side do I already know enough to settle that index for sure? Move that one. Container With Most Water made the same kind of choice.
Trace each step on paper on your own small example before coding, and check the total water by hand.

Pass from the right the same way, tallest after each index: 3, 3, 3, 2, 2, − (nothing after index 5).
Index 3 (height 3) beats the 2 on its left and the 2 on its right, so only that building qualifies. Index 0 has nothing on its left but loses to the 3 on its right.

blocks.title: Replication and consistency: lag, read-your-writes, CAP
blocks.builds_on: Day 6 · the single database as the next weak spot, Day 13 · stale data and TTLs in a cache, and Day 20 · PostgreSQL and transactions
points: Replication keeps copies of the same data on several machines: to survive a machine dying, to spread the reads, and to put data near users.

Leader and followers (also called primary and replicas): every write goes to the leader, which streams its log of changes to the followers; reads can go to any of them. This is the usual PostgreSQL and MySQL setup.

Synchronous: the leader waits for a follower to confirm before saying "committed", so a confirmed write survives the leader dying, but every write is slower and stalls if that follower is down. Asynchronous: the leader replies at once, which is fast, but the followers lag and a crash can lose the last writes. A common middle way is one synchronous follower and the rest asynchronous.
Replication lag: an asynchronous follower is usually milliseconds behind, but seconds or more under heavy load. A read from it can return old data, like a cache entry before its TTL ends (Day 13).

Read-your-writes: users must see their own changes. Send a user's reads to the leader for a short while after their own write, or always for their own data, and let everyone else read the followers. Pinning each user to one follower stops their view jumping back in time.

Failover: when the leader dies, a follower is promoted. Writes it hadn't received yet are lost, and if the old leader comes back still thinking it is the leader, two machines take writes (split brain). This needs a reliable way to decide the leader is really dead.

CAP: when the network splits the machines (a partition), the system must choose. Refuse requests it can't answer with the latest data (consistency), or answer with what it has, possibly stale (availability). Partitions will happen, so the real choice is C or A while one lasts.
Choose per feature, not per system: a seat booking or a payment favours consistency; a profile picture or a like count favours availability. Day 53 adds quorums, where several machines take writes.
blocks.say: I use a leader with asynchronous followers for reads, give users read-your-writes by sending their reads to the leader just after they write, and during a partition I choose consistency or availability per feature: payments refuse, profiles serve stale data.
example: Day 20's food app: one PostgreSQL leader and two followers. The 23 order writes a second go to the leader, and the 580 history reads a second are spread over the followers. Replication is asynchronous, usually under 100 ms behind.
Rahul places an order at 0 ms. At 50 ms the app loads "My orders" from a follower that is 300 ms behind during the dinner rush: the new order is missing. That is a read-your-writes failure.
Fix: for 10 seconds after a user's own write, longer than the worst lag you expect, send that user's reads to the leader. Everyone else keeps reading the followers.

The leader's machine dies and a follower is promoted. Orders confirmed in the last 300 ms may never have reached it, so they are lost. One synchronous follower means every confirmed order is on two machines first.
The link to the second data centre drops. Placing an order and taking payment must refuse in the cut-off side (consistency); showing menus and ratings serves what it has (availability).
In the interview, say it in that order: the replicas, the lag, how users see their own writes, what failover can lose, and the C-or-A choice for each feature.

selftest.q: Synchronous and asynchronous replication: what does each one give, and what does it cost?
selftest.a: Synchronous: a confirmed write is on two machines, so it survives the leader dying, but every write waits and stalls if that follower is down. Asynchronous: fast writes, but followers lag and a leader crash can lose the last writes.

selftest.q: What is read-your-writes, and how do you give it when reads go to followers?
selftest.a: Users always see their own changes. Send a user's reads to the leader for a short while after their own write (longer than the worst lag), or always for their own data, and let everyone else read the followers.

selftest.q: State CAP in one sentence, and say why "pick any two of three" misleads.
selftest.a: When a network partition splits the machines, a replicated system must either refuse some requests to stay consistent or answer them with possibly stale data. Partitions will happen anyway, so the real choice is consistency or availability while one lasts.

selftest.q: In a variable window, when is it safe to jump the left end instead of creeping?
selftest.a: When you can show that no window starting before the new position can ever win again. Say why before relying on it.

selftest.q: A cinema app runs in two regions and the link between them drops. What should seat booking do, and what should the film reviews do?
selftest.a: Seat booking chooses consistency: refuse bookings in the cut-off region rather than sell one seat twice. Reviews choose availability: show what that region has, even if a few minutes old.

blocks.title: Monthly checkpoint: cold re-solves + one design question
blocks.builds_on: Days 8 to 16 · Arrays & Hashing, and the month's HLD: Days 4, 6, 11, 13, 18, 20, 25 and 27
points: Once a month, about 90 minutes: four problems from Days 8–16, then one design question. It measures what has stuck, not what you could do on the day you learnt it.

Rules, as on Day 0: a blank file, no notes, no video and no old code. Before each problem, say the pattern, the brute force, the better idea and its Big-O, then start its timer. When the timer rings, stop and write one line on where you got stuck.
Score each problem like Day 0: 1 if it passes NeetCode's tests inside its timer, 0.5 if the idea was right but the code wasn't finished, 0 otherwise.

Rate each problem Easy, OK or Struggled in My notes. For OK or Struggled, make sure its bookmark is on (it may already be on from its first day), so it comes back after 1, 3, 7 and 21 days; Easy has stuck, so leave the bookmark as it is. If one is in today's Revise row, rate it there instead. Ticking it here only records today's checkpoint and leaves the original day's tick alone.

The design question, 25-minute cap, on paper and out loud. A good answer covers six things: the request journey and API, `POST /v1/urls` and `GET /{code}` answered with a redirect (Days 4 and 18); estimates of writes, reads and storage (Day 11); how codes are made, a counter or Snowflake id in base62 (Day 25); the database, lookups by code with the code as a unique key (Day 20); a cache-aside layer for hot codes with a TTL and LRU (Day 13); and followers for reads, with the creator's first click read from the leader (Day 27), behind stateless servers (Day 6). Score one point for each covered well.

Write the result in My notes as "Checkpoint 1: DSA x/4 · design x/6 · HLD x/5 · LLD x/5 · AI x/5", for example "Checkpoint 1: DSA 3.5/4 · design 4/6 · HLD 4/5 · LLD 3/5 · AI 3.5/5, missed estimates and replicas".

Then compare with Day 0. Re-answer Day 0's 15 quiz questions from memory, 2 minutes each, and score them the same way, so HLD, LLD and AI each get a number beside Day 0's. This re-take uses about 30 minutes of the catch-up time. Singleton, the parking lot and attention (LLD 4, LLD 5 and AI 5) come in Month 2, so expect those to stay low. Day 0's DSA was on unseen problems, so compare only how many you finished inside the timer. Say what moved, what didn't, and what Month 2 should push.

After the checkpoint, the rest of today is catch-up, with no set time: open any day from Days 1 to 27 that isn't marked done, finish what you skipped, and tap Mark day 28 done. If nothing is left, rest.
blocks.say: A month in, I check what has stuck by re-solving old problems cold and answering a design question under time, then I let the misses drive what comes back for revision.

selftest.q: Which pattern: in an unsorted list, find two numbers that add up to a target and return their positions?
selftest.a: A dict from value to index, asking for each number's complement before storing it (Day 9): O(n) time and O(n) memory.

selftest.q: Which pattern: in a sorted list, find two numbers that add up to a target with O(1) extra memory?
selftest.a: Two pointers from both ends: too small moves the left end on, too big moves the right end back (Day 23). O(n) time.

selftest.q: Which pattern: answer thousands of "total from index l to r" questions on a list that never changes?
selftest.a: Prefix sums (Day 15): build them once in O(n), then each answer is prefix[r + 1] − prefix[l] in O(1).

selftest.q: Which pattern: do two words use exactly the same letters, each the same number of times?
selftest.a: Count the letters of each with a dict or Counter and compare the counts (Day 9): O(n) time and at most 26 keys for lowercase letters. Sorting both words also works, in O(n log n).

selftest.q: Which pattern: count the subarrays that sum to k when the list has negative numbers?
selftest.a: Prefix sums plus a dict of how many times each prefix has appeared, asking about earlier prefixes before storing the current one (Day 18). A shrinking window fails with negatives (Day 3).

title: The variable window template · Embeddings and cosine similarity

blocks.title: Sliding Window: grow on the right, shrink on the left while the window breaks its rule
blocks.builds_on: Day 3 · longest_with_k_distinct and shrinking while the rule is broken, Day 26 · a count dict that deletes keys at 0, and Day 27 · moving the left end
points: Today the variable window gets a fixed template. For each right: add the item to the summary; while the window breaks its rule, remove the left item and move left on; then update the best with right − left + 1.
The summary is whatever lets you check the rule quickly: a count dict, a set or a running total (Day 26).
Before coding, write the rule in terms of the summary, in one line. Today's two problems have different rules; say each one out loud first.

The template needs one property: if a window follows the rule, every smaller window inside it does too. Then shrinking can always repair a broken window. Check it holds (Day 3: sums with negative numbers break it). Day 3 said the same thing the other way round: adding an item can never fix a broken window.
Each index enters the window once and leaves at most once, so it is O(n) despite the loop inside a loop.
Counting letters needs at most 26 keys, so the summary is O(1) memory, not O(n). Comparing or scanning it is O(26) per step.
Edge cases: an empty string, one character, every character the same, and a rule that the whole string already satisfies.
blocks.say: My variable window adds on the right, shrinks from the left while the rule is broken, and records the best after each step; each index enters and leaves once, so it's O(n), with a count summary of at most 26 letters.
example: Day 3's task, longest_with_k_distinct with k = 2, traced with the template: "abaccab". Rule: at most 2 different letters in the window.
right = 0 to 2 gives "aba": counts {a: 2, b: 1}, 2 different, so it follows the rule. Best 3.
right = 3 adds c: 3 different, broken. Shrink: drop a (a: 1), then drop b (b: 0, delete it). Now left = 2 and the window is "ac".
right = 4 and 5 give "acca": counts {a: 2, c: 2}. Best 4. right = 6 adds b: 3 different again, so shrink past a, c and c to left = 5: "ab".
Answer 4 ("acca"). Each index was added once and removed at most once: O(n).

blocks.title: Embeddings: things as vectors, cosine similarity
blocks.builds_on: Day 1 · features are numbers, and Day 3 · w1 × x1 + w2 × x2 + …, which multiplies two lists of numbers pairwise and adds them up
points: An embedding turns a thing (a word, a sentence, a product, a user) into a list of numbers, a vector, so that similar things get nearby vectors.

One-hot coding gives each word its own position, so every pair of words is equally far apart and "cat" is no closer to "kitten" than to "car". Embeddings are dense, with a few hundred numbers, and learnt so that distance means something.
They are learnt from data. word2vec learns from the words around each word; sentence models are trained so that matching pairs, such as a question and its answer, land close together.

The dot product a · b multiplies matching positions and adds them up. Cosine similarity = a · b ÷ (length of a × length of b): the cosine of the angle between them. 1 means the same direction, 0 unrelated, −1 opposite.

Cosine looks only at direction, not length. If every vector is first scaled to length 1 (normalised), cosine is just the dot product. With each vector as a row of a matrix E, `E @ E.T` puts the dot product of rows i and j at [i][j]: every similarity at once.
Semantic search: embed the documents once, embed the query, and return the top k by cosine. This is the retrieval step in RAG and in recommendations; Day 108 builds it properly.
Checking every stored vector costs O(n × d) per query, for n vectors of d numbers. At millions of vectors, an approximate nearest-neighbour index trades a little accuracy for speed.
Only compare vectors from the same model: two models' numbers mean different things. And similar is not the same as correct: a close match can still be the wrong answer.
blocks.say: An embedding maps text or items to vectors so that similar things point the same way; I compare them with cosine similarity, which after normalising is a dot product, and search by taking the top k.
example: Toy embeddings with 3 numbers (real ones have hundreds): cat = [0.9, 0.8, 0.1], kitten = [0.8, 0.9, 0.2], car = [0.1, 0.2, 0.9].
cosine(cat, kitten) = 1.46 ÷ (1.21 × 1.22) ≈ 0.99: almost the same direction.
cat · car = 0.09 + 0.16 + 0.09 = 0.34, and car's length ≈ 0.93, so cosine(cat, car) = 0.34 ÷ (1.21 × 0.93) ≈ 0.30: far apart.
[1.8, 1.6, 0.2] is cat doubled. Its cosine with cat is exactly 1.0: cosine ignores length and compares only direction.

selftest.q: In the variable window template, when does the left end move, and when do you update the best?
selftest.a: Left moves only while the window breaks its rule, one item at a time. The best is updated after the shrinking, once the window follows the rule again.

selftest.q: What property must the rule have for the template to work?
selftest.a: If a window follows the rule, every smaller window inside it does too. Then shrinking can always repair a broken window, and the pass stays O(n).

selftest.q: What is cosine similarity, and what do 1, 0 and −1 mean?
selftest.a: The dot product of two vectors divided by the product of their lengths: the cosine of the angle between them. 1 is the same direction, 0 is unrelated, −1 is opposite.

selftest.q: Why do many systems normalise embeddings to length 1?
selftest.a: Then cosine similarity is just the dot product, so one matrix multiply compares a query with every stored vector, and no lengths need computing per query.

selftest.q: What is the cosine of [1, 0] and [0, 1]? And of [1, 1] and [3, 3]?
selftest.a: [1, 0] · [0, 1] = 0, so the cosine is 0. [1, 1] and [3, 3] point the same way, so the cosine is 1, whatever their lengths.

title: Fixed windows with counts, shortest windows · Observer pattern

blocks.title: Sliding Window: fixed windows that compare counts, and the shortest valid window
blocks.builds_on: Day 29 · the variable window template, Day 26 · a fixed window with a count dict, and Day 9 · comparing Counters with ==
points: Two variations of the window today: a fixed size with a count summary, and a variable window that wants the shortest answer instead of the longest.
Fixed size from the question: when the input sets the window's length, the summary is not only updated at each step but also checked against a target summary. Two Counters compare with == (Day 9).

Over lowercase letters that comparison is O(26) per step, so the pass is O(26 × n) = O(n). A faster version keeps a running number of letters whose counts already match, but get the plain one working first.
Shortest instead of longest: the left end now moves for a different reason, to see how small a valid window can get. Trace the example to see where the answer is recorded.
Before coding, say whether the question wants the longest or the shortest window, and where the line that records the answer goes for that one.
The property from Day 29 still matters: with numbers ≥ 0, adding an item can only raise a sum, so a window that reached a target stays valid as it grows. Negative numbers break that (Day 18).
Edge cases: no valid window at all (return what the question asks, often 0), and a pattern longer than the text.
blocks.say: For a fixed-length match I slide a window of that length and compare counts in O(26) per step; for the shortest valid window I grow until valid, then shrink while it stays valid, recording the length inside the shrink loop.
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): days [0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 1, 0], where 1 means rain. Find the shortest run of days with at least 2 rainy days.
Grow right: at right = 4 the window 0–4 holds 2 rainy days, so it is valid: record 5. Shrink: drop day 0 (dry), still valid, record 4. Drop day 1 (rain): only 1 left, so stop with left = 2.
right = 5 makes it valid again: window 2–5, record 4. Drop days 2 and 3: windows 3–5 (3) and 4–5 (2). Dropping day 4 (rain) breaks it: left = 5.
right = 6 adds a dry day and the window 5–6 isn't valid. Best = 2, days 4–5.
Each day entered and left once: O(n). The answer was recorded inside the shrinking loop, the opposite of Day 29's longest window.

blocks.title: Observer pattern: tell subscribers when something changes
blocks.builds_on: Day 16 · Strategy, an interface whose objects are passed in, Day 9 · open/closed, and Day 21 · enums
points: Observer: a subject keeps a list of subscribers (observers) and calls each one when something changes. Observers subscribe and unsubscribe themselves; the subject never knows their concrete classes.
Its parts: the subject, with `subscribe(obs)`, `unsubscribe(obs)` and a notify loop; and an Observer interface, an ABC with one method such as `on_status(order_id, status)`.
Why: the thing that changes, such as an order, doesn't import the SMS, screen or analytics code. A new listener is one new class and one subscribe call, with no edits to the subject (Day 9).
Push or pull: pass the event's data in the call (push), or pass the subject and let each observer read what it needs (pull). Push is simpler; pull suits observers that need different fields.
In Python, an observer can also be a plain function: the subject keeps a list of callables, the same shortcut as Day 16's function strategies.

Pitfalls: one observer that raises shouldn't stop the rest, so catch, log and carry on; loop over a copy of the list, so an observer that unsubscribes mid-loop doesn't break it; and observers you forget to unsubscribe are never freed.
Strategy gives an object one swappable way to do its job; Observer lets many objects hear about one event. Across services, the same idea becomes publish/subscribe through a message queue (Day 39).
blocks.say: In the Observer pattern a subject keeps a list of subscribers and notifies each one through a small interface, so new reactions are new classes rather than edits, and one failing subscriber doesn't stop the others.
example: A food app: when an order's status changes, the customer gets an SMS, the restaurant's screen updates and analytics logs it. Order.set_status calls all three directly, so Order imports all their code.
Observer: `class OrderObserver(ABC)` with an abstract `on_status(order_id, status)`. Order keeps `self._observers = []` with `subscribe(obs)` and `unsubscribe(obs)`.
`set_status(new)` stores the status, then calls `obs.on_status(self.id, new)` for each obs in a copy of the list. Order never names SmsNotifier.
A delivery-partner app is one new observer class and one subscribe call; Order doesn't change (Day 9).
Test with a FakeObserver that appends each call to a list, then assert it received `("o42", Status.PICKED_UP)`, with Status an Enum (Day 21).

selftest.q: What are the parts of the Observer pattern?
selftest.a: A subject that keeps a list of observers, with subscribe, unsubscribe and a notify loop, and an observer interface with one method the subject calls on each change.

selftest.q: Why must one failing observer not stop the others, and how do you make sure of it?
selftest.a: The other observers did nothing wrong and still need the event. Catch the exception around each observer's call, log it and carry on with the rest.

selftest.q: Strategy and Observer: what is the difference?
selftest.a: Strategy: one object uses one swappable way to do its job. Observer: many objects are told about one event, and the subject doesn't know who they are.

selftest.q: Longest valid window and shortest valid window: where in the loop do you record the answer?
selftest.a: Longest: after shrinking until the window is valid again. Shortest: inside the shrinking loop, while the window is still valid, before each shrink.

selftest.q: Slide a window of 3 over "cbabca". Which start indexes hold exactly the letters of "abc"?
selftest.a: "cba" at 0 yes, "bab" at 1 no, "abc" at 2 yes, "bca" at 3 yes. So 0, 2 and 3.
